[[File:Kashima-jingu entrance.JPG|thumb|250px|right|{{Center|Otorii}}]]'''Kashima Jingu'''' (Kashima Jingu) is a {{ill|lt=Shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945|1=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|Q83273|qid=Q83273|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Kashima City|Q467471|qid=Q467471|1=Kashima, Ibaraki}}{{ill|lt=Imperial Palace (Kashima City)|Q11453223|qid=Q11453223|lt=Imperial Palace|1=Kyūchū}}. {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinai Shrine|1=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} ({{ill|lt=Meishin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964|1=Myōjin Taisha}}), {{ill|lt=Hitachikuni|Q1055353|qid=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}{{ill|lt=Ichinomiya|Q1656379|qid=Q1656379|1=Ichinomiya}}. {{ill|lt=Modern Shrine Ranking System|Q712534|comment=this used to link to modern system but that one is too overlinked|lt=Old Shrine Ranking|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}} is {{ill|lt=Modern Shrine Ranking System|Q712534|comment=this used to link to modern system but that one is too overlinked|lt=Old Shrine Ranking|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}} is {{ill|lt=Modern Shrine Ranking System#Government Shrine|Q712534|comment=this used to link to modern system but that one is too overlinked|lt=Kanpei Taisha|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}, and currently it is {{ill|lt=Beppyō Shrine|Q10898274|qid=Q10898274|1=Beppyo shrine}} of {{ill|lt=Shrine Head Office|Q908077|qid=Q908077|1=Association of Shinto Shrines}}.

Headquarters of {{ill|lt=Kashima Shrine|Q11677154|qid=Q11677154|1=Kashima Shrines}} located all over the country. {{ill|lt=Katori Shrine|Q372380|qid=Q372380|1=Katori Jingū}} in {{ill|lt=Chiba Prefecture|Q80011|qid=Q80011|1=Chiba Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Katori City|Q858357|qid=Q858357|1=Katori, Chiba}}, {{ill|lt=Kamisu City|Q840595|qid=Q840595|1=Kamisu}} in Ibaraki Prefecture Along with {jalink|Ikusu Shrine|Q11073095}}, it is one of the {{ill|lt=Togokusansha|Q17222093|qid=Q17222093|1=Tōgoku Sansha}}<ref>[http://www.kamisu-kanko.jp/power/ Togoku Sansha] (Kamisu City Tourism Association). </ref>. It is also a shrine that is worshiped from a distance in the {{ill|lt=four directions|Q11419901|qid=Q11419901|1=Shihohai}} of the imperial court.

=== Overview ===
It is located on Kashima {{ill|lt=plateau|Q75520|qid=Q75520|1=Plateau}} in the southeastern part of Ibaraki Prefecture, sandwiched between {{ill|lt=Kitaura|Q11402369|qid=Q11402369|1=Kitaura}} and {{ill|lt=Kashima-nada|Q11677147|qid=Q11677147|1=Kashima Sea}}. It is one of the oldest shrines in eastern Japan, and its enshrinement is confirmed in the ``{{ill|lt=Hitachikuni Fudoki|Q11481687|qid=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}'', and it is said to have been enshrined in {{ill|lt=Japanese mythology|Q814158|qid=Q814158|1=Japanese mythology}}. It is known for enshrining {{ill|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi|Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchijin|1=Takemikazuchi}} (Takemikazuchi, Takemikazuchi), who played an active role in the pacification of Ashihara China||the transfer of the country of the great lords}}. Since {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hitachi|1=UNKNOWN}} was the northern tip of the ancient national territory, Kashima Shrine, which enshrines the god Takemikazuchi who followed the descendants of the heavens and subdued the country, was valued as the guardian deity of the northern part of the nation. 9 “Hitachi’s Religious World and Muzhu” Sumio Kameyama</ref>. In {{ill|lt=Ancient|Q41493|qid=Q41493|1=Ancient history}}, he was revered by the imperial court as the Heidadokami of Emishi, and by the {{ill|lt=Fujiwara clan|Q641628|qid=Q641628|1=Fujiwara clan}} as {{ill|lt=guardian deity|Q767655|qid=Q767655|1=Ujigami}}. His divine authority continued even after he passed into the {{ill|lt=samurai class|Q2927809|qid=Q2927809|1=Buke}} world in {{ill|lt=Middle Ages|Q12554|qid=Q12554|1=Middle Ages}}, and was revered as {{ill|lt=God of War|Q11124822|qid=Q11124822|1=武神}} by successive samurai governments. Even today, it is a shrine that is deeply worshiped in {{ill|lt=martial arts|Q752021|qid=Q752021|1=Budō}}.Among the cultural properties, a long {{ill|lt=straight sword|Q63821|qid=Q63821|1=Chokutō}} called ``{{ill|lt=Futomitama|Q11059754|qid=Q11059754|lt=Futunomitama no Tsurugi|1=Futsu-no-mitama}}'' has been designated as a {{ill|lt=National Treasure|Q1139795|qid=Q1139795|1=National Treasure (Japan)}}. Also, the precincts are national {{ill|lt=historic sites|Q1081138|qid=Q1081138|1=Historic site}}, {{ill|lt=main shrine|Q2044994|qid=Q2044994|1=Honden}}, {{ill|lt=haiden|Q3125745|qid=Q3125745|1=Haiden (Shinto)}}, {{j Seven of the shrine buildings, including alink|Roumon|Q97378762}}, have been designated as national {{ill|lt=Important Cultural Properties|Q1188622|qid=Q1188622|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}}, and many other cultural properties have been preserved to this day. It is also known that {{ill|lt=deer|Q23390|qid=Q23390|lt=deer|1=Deer}} is considered {{ill|lt=divine messenger|Q10444973|qid=Q10444973|1=Shinshi}}.

=== Company name ===
The shrine is located in {{ill|lt=Hitachi Province|Q1055353|qid=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}{{ill|lt=Kashima District (Hitachi Province)|UNKNOWN|lt=Kashima District}}, and the place name "Kashima" is derived from "{{ill|lt=Hitachi Province Fudoki|Q11481687|qid=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}" <ref group="Hara" In name="Fudoki"/>, it is written as "'''Koshima''''{{Sfn|Kashima County (Heibonsha)|1982}}. In the Fudoki, it is explained that the name of ``Koshima County'' is based on ``Koshima's Ten no Okami'' (referring to Kashima Shrine) {{Sfn|Kashima County (Kadokawa)|1983}}. The first mention of ``Kashima'' as ``''Kashima'''' is in {{ill|lt=Yoro|Q1373061|qid=Q1373061|1=Yōrō}} 7 ({{ill|lt=723|Q23545|qid=Q23545|1=723}})<ref group="Hara">Shoku Nihongi, November 16th, Yoro 7th year (723). </ref>, {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=14}}, and it is believed that the name was changed from ``Koshima'' to ``Kashima'' in the early 8th century {{Sfn|Kashima County (Heibonsha)|1982}}. The reason for this change is not clear from historical documents, but the shrine explains that it originates from the deer of the divine messenger {{Sfn|Shikaen (Kashima Jingu Official Website)}}. There are various theories about the origin of this word "Kashima". The main theory is as follows.
* Theory that it is "God's address" or "Kasumi" {{Sfn|Kashima District (Kadokawa)|1983}}
* The theory is that "Kashima" was taken from {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kenturuma no Mikoto|1=UNKNOWN}} (Takekashima no Mikoto){{Sfn|Kashima District (Kadokawa)|1983}}*: Kenruma no Mikoto (Kenruma Mikoto) is "{{ill|lt=Sendai Kojihonki|Q2716751|qid=Q2716751|1=Kujiki}}" Kokuzohonki<ref group="hara">'Sendai Kojihonki' and "Kokuzohonki" Nakakunizojo. </ref> as the first {{ill|lt=Nakakunizo|Q11378492|qid=Q11378492|1=Naka no Kuni no Miyatsuko}} (Nakakunizo), and a person whose description can be seen in the "Hitachi Province Fudoki" <ref group="Hara" name="Namegata District"/>.
* The theory is that it is "Kashishima" which means "a place where pegs are driven to stop ships" {{Sfn|Kashima District (Kadokawa)|1983}}
*: "{{ill|lt=Hizen Province Fudoki|Q111890610|qid=Q111890610|1=Hizen no Kuni Fudoki}}" <ref group="Hara">``Hizen Province Fudoki'' {{ill|lt=Kishima District|Q1044239|qid=Q1044239|1=Kishima District, Saga}} article. Based on the description that appears to be the origin of "Kishima" in </ref>{{Sfn|Kashima District (Kadokawa)|1983}}.

Although Jingu currently uses the character ``shima'' in its company name, the local government of Kashima City, Ibaraki Prefecture uses the character ``shima'' to distinguish it from {{ill|lt=Saga Prefecture|Q160420|qid=Q160420|1=Saga Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Kashima City|Q684494|qid=Q684494|1=Kashima, Saga}}.

=== Enshrined God ===
[[File:Kashima-kanameishi-shinzu-namazu-e.jpg|thumb|180px|right|{{Center|``Kashima Kanameishi Shinzu''}}{{Small|{{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963|1=Edo period}} {{ill|lt=catfish painting|Q11674298|qid=Q11674298|1=namazu-e}}. The top one is Kashima Shrine, which enshrines the {{ill|lt=Keystone|Q11630053|qid=Q11630053|1=Kaname-ishi}}, and the bottom one is the {{ill|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi|Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi God|1=Takemikazuchi}} holding a sword and holding down a large catfish. }}]]
The following deities are enshrined:
* '''{{ill|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi|Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi Okami|1=Takemikazuchi}}''' (Takemikazuchi no Okami<ref name="Yoshisho"/>/Takemikazuchi no Okami{{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=8}})
*: In "{{ill|lt=Kojiki|Q813031|qid=Q813031|1=Kojiki}}" he is written as "Takemikaraijin" and in "{{ill|lt=Nihonshoki|Q813935|qid=Q813935|1=Nihon Shoki}}" he is written as "Takemikazuchijin" {{Sfn|Takemikazuchijin (National History)|1988}}.
*: Also known as ``Takefutsu no Kami'' and ``Toyofutsu no Kami'' {{Sfn|Takemikazujin (National History)|1988}}.

=== About the enshrined deity ===
As mentioned above, the main deity enshrined at Kashima Shrine is said to be {{ill|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi|Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|1=Takemikazuchi}} (Takemikazuchi/Takemikazuchi). The origin of Takemikazuchi is described in the Kojiki <ref group="Hara" name="Kojiki">Kojiki Jindaiki. In </ref>, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Izanagi no Mikoto|1=UNKNOWN}} (Izanagi no Mikoto) cut off the head of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hinokarugutsuchi|1=UNKNOWN}} (Kugatsuchi), and the blood on the sword splattered on the rock, making him one of three gods. group="Hara">Jindaiki of Nihonshoki.</ref>This is where Takemikazuchi's ancestor {{ill|lt=Mikahayahi|Q11574224|qid=Q11574224|lt=Mikahayahi|1=Mika-haya-hi}} was born. Also, in the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ashihara Chugoku pacification|1=UNKNOWN}} that preceded the {{ill|lt=Descent of the Tenson|Q1084733|qid=Q1084733|1=Tenson kōrin}}, he is said to have played an active role together with {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Amenotrifune|1=UNKNOWN}} (Amenotrifune}} (Amenotrifune deity: Kojiki) or {{ill|lt=Ketsunushikami|Q1107286|qid=Q1107286|1=Futsunushi}} (Nihon Shoki).{{Sfn|Tozane|2000|p=48}}. Afterwards, on the occasion of {{ill|lt=Jinmu Tosei|Q11590444|qid=Q11590444|1=Jimmu's Eastern Expedition}}, Takemikazuchi bestowed the divine sword ({{ill|lt=Futo Mitama|Q11059754|qid=Q11059754|1=Futsu-no-mitama}}) on Rebiko Ibara ({{ill|lt=Emperor Jinmu|Q200188|qid=Q200188|1=Emperor Jimmu}}) {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=8}}. However, there is no mention of Kashima Jingu in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, so the relationship between Takemikazuchi and Kashima is unclear {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Gods)|1984}}.On the other hand, in "Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki" <ref group="Hara" name="Fudoki"/>, the deity enshrined at Kashima Jingu Shrine is described as ``'''Kashima's great god of heaven'''' (Kashima no Ame no Okami), and this deity is said to have descended from heaven before the reign of the Tensons, and the legend is similar to the legend in the Kiki.{{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Kadokawa)|1983}}. However, there is no mention of this god being Takemikazuchi in the Fudoki {{Sfn|Ichinomiya system|2000|p=230}}.
{{Quotation|The great god who descended from the field of high heavens, his name is ``The Great God of Koshima Heaven.'' In the heavens, it is named Sunahachi Hi-no-Kojima-no-miya, and in earth it is named Sunahachi-Toyokajima-no-miya. |Excerpt from "{{ill|lt=Hitachikuni Fudoki|Q11481687|qid=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}" Kojima Gunjo (original text in Chinese) <ref>The text is based on "New Edition of Japanese Classical Literature Complete Works 5 Fudoki", Shogakukan, 2003 (Japan Knowledge Edition), pp. 389-390. </ref>}}The first reference to a document stating that Takemikazuchi is the enshrined deity of the shrine is in ``{{ill|lt=Kogo Shui|Q531555|qid=Q531555|1=Kogo Shūi}}'' <ref group="Hara">``Kogo Shui'' (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref> (established in {{ill|lt=807|Q30016|qid=Q30016|1=807}}), there is a description that ``Takemikazuchijin and so on, now Kashimakami Koreya in Hitachi Province'' {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. However, "Kasuga Festival Norito" in "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" (composed in {{ill|lt=927|Q30470|qid=Q30470|1=927}})<ref group="original">"Engishiki" Volume 8 Norito Kasuga Festival article (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref> also appears as ``Kashima Zaken Oga Mamechi no Mikoto,'' but this ``Kasuga Festival Norito'' was written in {{ill|lt=Jingo Keiun|Q1373049|qid=Q1373049|1=Jingo-keiun}} 2nd year ({{ill|lt=768th year|Q29961|qid=Q29961|1=768}}), which is said to be the founding of Kasuga Taisha Shrine.<ref group="Note" There is a theory that it dates back to name="Kasuga"/>{{Sfn|Akira Fujisawa|1994}}. Based on the above, there is a theory that the deity of Takemikazuchi, the war god in the central mythology, was added to the local deity "Koshimakami" as the Ezo was conquered from {{ill|lt=8th century|Q8086|qid=Q8086|1=8th century}}. n|Kiichi Kushida|2014}}, there is a theory that the central land transfer myth itself was created by the Nakatomi clan interfering with the "Koshima deity" that descended to Hitachi.<ref>{{ill|lt=Ken Matsumae|Q11529297|qid=Q11529297|1=Takeshi Matsumae}} “A book that helps you understand the mysteries of Japanese mythology” Yamato Shobo, 2007, pp. 126-129. </ref>.The deity enshrined at the shrine is considered to have the characteristics of a war god or war god, based on the story in the Kiki that Takemikazuchi played an active role in pacifying the land and the Fudoki that he dedicated arms to him. </ref>. In particular, regarding the other names "Takefutsu" and "Toyofutsu", the name "Hutsu" is said to be a word representing "the sharpness of a sword", as seen in the name of the divine sword {{ill|lt=Futomitama|Q11059754|qid=Q11059754|lt=Futsunomitama|1=Futsu-no-mitama}} (Futomitama/Hanirei), so there is a theory that it is a god symbolizing swords.<ref name="Takemikarai">{{ill|lt=Ken Matsumae|Q11529297|qid=Q11529297|1=Takeshi Matsumae}} "Takemikazujin" (``National History Encyclopedia'', Yoshikawa Kobunkan). </ref>. An example of the recognition that Kashima Jingu is the god of war is "{{ill|lt=Ryojin Hisho|Q3010584|qid=Q3010584|1=Ryōjin Hishō}}" ({{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292|1=Heian period}} "The shrine of Kashima, the god of war east of Seki, {{ill|lt=Katori Shrine|Q372380|qid=Q372380|lt=Katori|1=Katori Jingū}}, {{ill|lt=Suwa Taisha|Q218813|qid=Q218813|lt=Suwa|1=Suwa-taisha}}" <ref group="Hara">"Ryojin Hisho" Volume 2 Shiku Shinka. </ref> is known as {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. On the other hand, there are also indications that he was a god of navigation, as the Fudoki describes him as a god of navigation, {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Kadokawa)|1983}}, and that he is a god of agriculture, as the Fudoki describes him as a ritual group, {{ill|lt=Urabe clan|Q11409028|qid=Q11409028|lt=Uji|1=Urabe clan}}, who dug a well.{{Sfn|Akira Fujisawa|1994}}. Looking at the above, there is a theory that he had a complex personality such as a god of war, a god of navigation, and a god of agriculture.{{Sfn|Akira Fujisawa|1994}} On the other hand, there is a genealogy that connects Takemikazuchi and the distant ancestor of the Nakatomi clan, {{ill|lt=Amagiya no Mikoto|Q2564508|qid=Q2564508|1=Ame-no-Koyane}}, and successive generations of the Nakatomi clan also include Tsuhayasan Reimichi and Ichisenkon Mikoto. , {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ikazuomi no Mikoto|1=UNKNOWN}}, {{ill|lt=Nakatomi Ujitsu|Q55536814|qid=Q55536814|lt=Raidain no Mikoto|1=Nakatomi no Ikatsu}}, and other divine and personal names related to "thunder" can be found. {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kikokuzō|1=UNKNOWN}}, who is considered to be the same ancestor of the clan, also has divine names related to thunder, such as the Raijin ritual ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Narirai Shrine|1=UNKNOWN}}) and Tenrai no Mikoto. There is also a theory that Takemikazuchi is considered to be the original god of the Nakatomi clan. Descendants of ancient Urabe who were responsible for fortune-telling,” Aogaki Publishing, 2014, pp. 40-43. </ref>.

=== Features ===
[[File:Katori-jingu haiden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|{{ill|lt=Katori Shrine|Q372380|qid=Q372380|1=Katori Jingū}} ({{ill|lt=Chiba Prefecture|Q80011|qid=Q80011|1=Chiba Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Katori City|Q858357|qid=Q858357|1=Katori, Chiba}})}}{{Small|{{ill|lt=Shimosa Province|Q1053695|qid=Q1053695|1=Shimōsa Province}}{{ill|lt=Ichinomiya|Q1656379|qid=Q1656379|1=Ichinomiya}}. It has a deep relationship with Kashima Jingu, and has been called the same name since ancient times. }}]]
Kashima Shrine is located in '''{{ill|lt=Katori Shrine|Q372380|qid=Q372380|1=Katori Jingū}}'' ({{ill|lt=Chiba Prefecture|Q80011|qid=Q80011|1=Chiba Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Katori City|Q858357|qid=Q858357|1=Katori, Chiba}}, {{Coord |35|53|10.03|N|140|31|43.27|E|region:JP-12_type:landmark|name=Shimousa-kuni Ichinomiya: Katori Shrine}})), it has a deep relationship with Kashima and Katori Shrine since ancient times, and is considered a pair along with Kashima and Katori. 76. </ref>.Both Kashima and Katori Shrines are deeply revered shrines that have been deeply revered by the {{ill|lt=Imperial Court (Japan)|Q30253177|qid=Q30253177|lt=Imperial Court|1=Imperial Court of Japan}} since ancient times. The reason behind this divine power is that both shrines were worshiped as gods of war.<ref name="Q5"/> In ancient eastern Kanto, present-day {{ill|lt=Kasumigaura|Q1077984|qid=Q1077984|1=Lake Kasumigaura}} (Nishiura, {{ill|lt=Kitaura|Q11402369|qid=Q11402369|1=Kitaura}}), {{ill|lt=Inbanuma|Q5120731|qid=Q5120731|1=Inbanuma}}, and {{jalink|Tega The {{ill|lt=Inland Sea|Q2578218|qid=Q2578218|1=Inland sea}}, called the {{ill|lt=Inland Sea|Q2578218|qid=Q2578218|1=Inland sea}}, extends throughout the area including the swamp|Q3215223}}, and both shrines are located in topographically important areas that block the entrance to it. This Katori Sea is thought to have functioned as a transportation base for the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yamato administration|1=UNKNOWN}}'s advance into {{ill|lt=Ezo|Q932574|qid=Q932574|1=Emishi}}. </ref>, both shrines were considered to be their strongholds, and the {{ill|lt=branch spirits|Q195793|qid=Q195793|1=Bunrei}} of both shrines were enshrined in various places along the Tohoku coast as gods representing the power of the imperial court ({{ill|lt=#Kashima Naesenjin|UNKNOWN|lt=described later}}). The main shrine building of Kashima Jingu faces north, which is said to be a design with Ezo in mind.

The following examples show the importance the Imperial Court attaches to it.
* {{ill|lt=Kamigun|Q11590937|qid=Q11590937|1=Kamigun}}*: Kashima and Katori Jingu Shrines, respectively {{ill|lt=Hitachikuni|Q1055353|qid=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}{{ill|lt=Kashima County (Ibaraki Prefecture)|Q6374307|qid=Q6374307|lt=Kashima County|1=Kashima District, Ibaraki}}, {{ill|lt=Shimosa Province|Q1053695|qid=Q1053695|1=Shimōsa Province}}{{ill|lt=Katori County|Q780284|qid=Q780284|1=Katori District}} was designated as Kami-gun, that is, the entire county was designated as divine territory.{{Sfn|Seiji Okada|2011}} group="Original">Volume 16 of "Ryoshuikai" Selected Ordinance Doji Juden Article/Fugyo 3rd Grade and Higher Parents </ref> and {{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}<ref name="Shikibujo" group="Original"/>). There are few examples of shrines with shrines, and all of them are said to have been important locations for military and transportation {{Sfn|Seiji Okada|2011}}.
* Envoy Kashima Katori
*: Every year, the Imperial Court sent Kashima envoys and Katori envoys, or simply Kashima Katori envoys, to both shrines {{Sfn|Seiji Okada|2011}}. At shrines in regions other than {{ill|lt=Ise Province|Q864166|qid=Q864166|lt=Ise|1=Ise Province}} and {{ill|lt=Kinki region|Q164256|qid=Q164256|lt=Kinki|1=Kansai region}}, imperial envoys are not regularly dispatched except for the two shrines. {{ill|lt=Usa Jingu|Q715632|qid=Q715632|1=Usa Jingū}} (once every six years), and both Kashima and Katori Shrines were extremely unusual {{Sfn|Seiji Okada|2011}}.
* Name of "{{ill|lt=Jingu|Q120680118|qid=Q120680118|1=List of Jingū}}"*: In "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" {{ill|lt=Engishiki Shinmyocho|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932|lt=Shinmyocho|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō}} ({{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292|1=Heian period}} {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Government shrines|1=UNKNOWN}} list), "Jingu" Only three shrines were labeled as Daijingu ({{ill|lt=Ise Jingu|Q687168|qid=Q687168|1=Ise Grand Shrine}}{{ill|lt=Kodaijingu|Q11581011|qid=Q11581011|lt=Naiku|1=Kōtai Jingū}}), Kashima Jingu, and Katori Jingu.{{Sfn|Seiji Okada|2011}}<ref group="Note">Before the Heian period, other examples of the use of the name ``Jingu'' include ``{{ill|lt=Ishigami Jingu|Q708859|qid=Q708859|1=Isonokami Jingū}}'' in ``Kojiki'' and ``Nihon Shoki,'' but in the ``Engishiki'' shrine name book, it is written as ``Ishigami Zaburomitama Shrine'' {{Harv|Seiji Okada|2011}}. </ref>.

[[File:Kamatari-jinja honden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Kamatari Shrine (Miyanaka, Kashima City)}}{{Small|{{ill|lt=Fujiwara Kamatari|Q433995|qid=Q433995|1=Fujiwara no Kamatari}}'s birthplace. }}]]Also, one of his characteristics is the veneration he receives from {{ill|lt=Fujiwara clan|Q641628|qid=Q641628|1=Fujiwara clan}}. In Kashima, there are many legends about the predecessor of the Fujiwara clan, {{ill|lt=Nakatomi clan|Q1198447|qid=Q1198447|1=Nakatomi clan}}, but the founder of the Fujiwara clan, {{ill|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari|Q433995|qid=Q433995|1=Fujiwara no Kamatari}}, also has a deep relationship with Hitachi, and is written in the Kuji-gun section of the Hitachi Province Fudoki. According to </ref>, a fiefdom was established in Hitachi Province under Kamatari (Fujiwara's Minister of the Interior). Also, ``{{ill|lt=Great Mirror|Q385120|qid=Q385120|1=Ōkagami}}'' (late Heian period)<ref group="hara">``Great Mirror'' Volume 2: Tales of the Fujiwara clan. There is also a theory that Kamatari was born in Hitachi Province based on </ref> for the first time. 40|37|5.41|E|region:JP-08_type:landmark|name=Kamatari Shrine (Fujiwara Kamatari birth place)}}) is said to be his birthplace.{{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=135}}. At {{ill|lt=Kasuga Taisha|Q714559|qid=Q714559|1=Kasuga-taisha}} in {{ill|lt=Nara|Q11444975|qid=Q11444975|1=Nara}}, which was founded as a shrine for the Fujiwara clan, Kashima-jin is enshrined in the first shrine and Katori-jin is enshrined in the second shrine.<ref name="Kasuga"/>, was ranked higher than {{ill|lt=Amagiya no Mikoto|Q2564508|qid=Q2564508|lt=Amagoyane no Mikoto|1=Ame-no-Koyane}} (Third Hall), the ancestor god of the Fujiwara clan, but was the father of Amagoyane no Mikoto. There is a theory that Takemikaraijin is <ref>{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Matoshi Suzuki|1=UNKNOWN}} ``Izu Sukune Genealogy'' and ``Hyakke Keizhuho'' Book 1</ref>, and according to this theory, Takemikazujin is the ancestor of the Nakatomi clan.After that, even after the samurai entered the world in the Middle Ages, both shrines were worshiped by the samurai as shrines that enshrined the god of war. Even in modern times, faith in {{ill|lt=martial arts|Q4867842|qid=Q4867842|1=武術}} is strong, and dojos often display paired hanging scrolls with the words ``Kashima Daimyojin'' and ``Katori Daimyojin'' written on them.

=== History ===

=== Founding/Tradition ===
Regarding the establishment, the history of Kashima Jingu Shrine "Kashima Shrine Biography" ({{ill|lt=Kamakura period|Q236205|qid=Q236205|1=Kamakura period}}) and ancient documents ({{ill|lt=Oei|Q1193078|qid=Q1193078|1=Ōei}}32 ({{ill|lt=1425|Q6283|qid=Q6283|1=1425}})) It is said that the first shrine pillar was built in the first year of {{ill|lt=Emperor Jinmu|Q200188|qid=Q200188|1=Emperor Jimmu}} {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Shikiuchi Shrine)|1976}}, and the shrine side considers the first year of Emperor Jimmu to be the year of its foundation {{Sfn|Jingu Journal|2004|p=9}}.On the other hand, the history of the shrine is also described in ``{{ill|lt=Hitachikuni Fudoki|Q11481687|qid=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}'' <ref group="Hara" name="Fudoki"/>, which states that the ``Great God of Heaven of Koshima'' descended from Takamagahara to the shrine of Koshima {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. It is also said that ``Ama no Okami of Kojima'' is a general term for three shrines: Ten no Okami Shrine (currently Kashima Shrine), Sakado Shrine (currently Sessha Sakado Shrine), and Numao Shrine (currently Sessha Numao Shrine) {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Later, during the reign of the 10th Emperor Sujin, {{ill|lt=Emperor Sujin|Q333530|qid=Q333530|1=Emperor Sujin}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1=UNKNOWN}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1=UNKNOWN}}, received an oracle from the Kashima deity at Mt. Osaka on Mt. Osaka. Furthermore, during the reign of the 12th Emperor Keiko|Q329723}, {{ill|lt=Omi Sayama no Mikoto|Q99517230|qid=Q99517230|lt=Nakatomi Omi Sayama no Mikoto|1=Omikiyama no Mikoto}} was sent to the oracle of the great god of heaven. It is said that three boats were dedicated there, and this is said to be the origin of the {{ill|lt=#Shikinen-sai|UNKNOWN|lt=Mifune-sai}} (Shikinen-daisai) {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}.Ominosayama-no-Mikoto participated in {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Waken-no-Mikoto|1=UNKNOWN}}'s eastern expedition activities, and the distribution of Kashima-kami and Kashima-miko-kami, which are often seen in the Mutsu region, seems to be due to the fact that the ancestors of the Nakatomi clan and members of the tribe accompanied and engaged in the eastern expedition activities. In addition, there is a theory that the dedication of the boat that appears in the Fudoki was actually presented during the eastern expedition of Wa Kenmei. Descendants of ancient Urabe who were responsible for fortune-telling,” Aogaki Publishing, 2014, pp. 35-37. </ref>.

=== Outline ===

==== Asuka era ====
In "Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki" <ref group="Hara" name="Fudoki"/>, it can be seen that many {{ill|lt=Kobe (Private)|Q11589711|qid=Q11589711|lt=Kobe|1=Kanbe (social class)}}, that is, attached private houses for maintaining rituals, were installed at Kashima Shrine {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Furthermore, in the Fudoki, in {{ill|lt=Taika|Q1077930|qid=Q1077930|1=Taika (era)}}5 ({{ill|lt=649|Q31117|qid=Q31117|1=649}}), it was named as {{ill|lt=Kamigun|Q11590937|qid=Q11590937|1=Kamigun}}. (Ibaraki Prefecture|Q6374307|Kashima County}}) was established for {{ill|lt=Emperor Tenji|Q314802|qid=Q314802|1=Emperor Tenji}} ({{jalink|668 years|Q30116} }-{{ill|lt=672|Q30601|qid=Q30601|1=672}}), it is said that a messenger was sent for the first time to construct the shrine.{{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. The background to the above is thought to be the strengthening of the imperial court's management of the eastern part of the country by the new government after the {{ill|lt=Taika Reform|Q570140|qid=Q570140|1=Taika Reform}}, and with the reform, the imperial court deepened its ties with Kashima Shrine, and the construction of the shrine by the Tenchi dynasty is considered to be a major breakthrough {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}.It has been pointed out that the existence of {{ill|lt=Nakatomi clan|Q1198447|qid=Q1198447|1=Nakatomi clan}} was behind this connection with the imperial court {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. The Nakatomi clan reorganized the ritual system from the late {{ill|lt=6th century|Q8090|qid=Q8090|1=6th century}} to the early {{ill|lt=7th century|Q8089|qid=Q8089|1=7th century}}, and along with this, the Nakatomi clan and Urabe clan were established in Togoku. He is said to have established the {{ill|lt=bumin system|Q2892644|qid=Q2892644|lt=bumin|1=Bemin}} and took control of the rituals of Kashima Shrine, which was a local deity.{{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. In fact, in historical materials there are many Kashima Gunji and shrine priests with the surname Nakatomi {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. After the Taika Reforms, the Nakatomi clan made great strides politically, and Kashima Shrine also deepened its relationship with the Imperial Court.{{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. There are various theories about the clans that performed rituals before the Nakatomi clan entered the country, but it is not clear (see section ``{{ill|lt=#Research|UNKNOWN|lt=Research}}'').Examples of how Kashima no Kami played a major role in the imperial court's management of the eastern region include the later "{{ill|lt=Nihon Sandai Jiroku|Q1052981|qid=Q1052981|1=Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku}}" <ref name="Jōgan 8" group="Hara"/> and "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" {{ill|lt=Engishiki Shinmeicho|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932|lt=Shinmeicho|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō}}<ref group="Hara" name="Mutsu"/>, it has been pointed out that there are many seedling deities ({{ill|lt=Mikogami|Q352176|qid=Q352176|1=Mikogami}}) of Kashima deities in Mutsu Province {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}} (see section "{{ill|lt=#Kashima Seedling God|UNKNOWN|lt=Kashima Seedling God}}"). From this description, it is said that Kashima no kami moved north along the Pacific coast as a god of war and water for the pacification of the country, and in the process was enshrined in various settlements, ultimately exerting influence as far as present-day {{ill|lt=Miyagi Prefecture|Q47896|qid=Q47896|1=Miyagi Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Ishinomaki City|Q270814|qid=Q270814|1=Ishinomaki}}{{Sfn|Kashima Migo Shrine (National History)|1983}}.

==== Nara period ====
[[File:Kasuga-taisha11bs3200.jpg|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|{{ill|lt=Kasuga Taisha|Q714559|qid=Q714559|1=Kasuga-taisha}} ({{ill|lt=Nara Prefecture|Q131287|qid=Q131287|1=Nara Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Nara City|Q169134|qid=Q169134|1=Nara (city)}})}}{{Small|Fujiwara clan's shrine. At the time of its construction, the god Takemikazuchi was sent to Kasuga from Kashima and enshrined in its first hall. }}]]In the {{ill|lt=Nara period|Q189178|qid=Q189178|1=Nara period}}, there are many articles about {{ill|lt=Kobe (Minbe)|Q11589711|qid=Q11589711|lt=Kobe|1=Kanbe (social class)}} in history books (see section "{{ill|lt=#sharyo|UNKNOWN|lt=sharyo}}"). Also, during this period, Kashima Shrine was especially revered as {{ill|lt=tutelary deity|Q767655|qid=Q767655|1=Ujigami}} by {{ill|lt=Fujiwara clan|Q641628|qid=Q641628|1=Fujiwara clan}}. {{ill|lt=Jingo Keiun|Q1373049|qid=Q1373049|1=Jingo-keiun}}2 ({{ill|lt=768|Q29961|qid=Q29961|1=768}}) was {{ill|lt=Nara Prefecture|Q131287|qid=Q131287|lt=Nara|1=Nara Prefecture}}{{jalink|Mt. Kasuga (Nara Prefecture)|Q11513602|Kasuga Shrine (currently {{ill|lt=Kasuga Taisha|Q714559|qid=Q714559|1=Kasuga-taisha}}) is said to have been founded as a family shrine of the Fujiwara clan on Mt. Mt. Mt.<ref group="Note" name="Kasuga">The exact year of the founding of Kasuga Shrine is not clear. ``Jingo Keiun 2nd Year'' is based on the shrine diary of Kasuga Taisha Shrine, and is supported by the article dated August 26, 1988 in the ``Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku'' (Kasuga Taisha Shrine section of ``Kokushi Daijiten''). </ref>, Takemotsuchi no Mikoto (First Hall) from Kashima, Tsunetsu Nushi no Mikoto (Second Hall) from Katori, {{ill|lt=Amagiya no Mikoto|Q2564508|qid=Q2564508|lt=Amagoyane no Mikoto|1=Ame-no-Koyane}} (Third Hall) and {{ill|lt=Hime God|Q22070227|qid=Q22070227|1=Himegami}} (Fourth Hall) from {{ill|lt=Hiraoka Shrine|Q32422|qid=Q32422|lt=Hiraoka|1=Hiraoka Shrine}} were solicited. name="Kasuga">{{ill|lt=Eizo Inagaki|Q11596499|qid=Q11596499|1=Eizō Inagaki}}"Kasuga Taisha" ("National History Dictionary", Yoshikawa Kobunkan). </ref>. Among these four deities, Kasuga no Kami is the main deity, and the original rituals of Kasuga Shrine are thought to have originated from distant worship at Kasuga Shrine <ref name="Kasuga"/>. Even after that, the relationship with the Fujiwara clan was deep, and Hoki 8th year ({{ill|lt=777th year|Q30714|qid=Q30714|1=AD 777}})<ref group="Hara" When {{ill|lt=Fujiwara Yoshitsugu|Q11623505|qid=Q11623505|1=Fujiwara no Yoshitsugu}} of name="Houki 8"/> was ill, the Seisanmi rank {{ill|lt=Divine Rank|Q11591025|qid=Q11591025|1=Shinkai (divine rank)}} was dedicated to Kashima Shrine, his ``guardian deity'' {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Kadokawa)|1983}}.

==== Heian period ====
The divine rank after {{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292|1=Heian period}} is {{ill|lt=Jowa (Japan)|Q1075605|qid=Q1075605|lt=Jowa|1=Jōwa (Heian period)}}3 ({{ill|lt=836|Q24957|qid=Q24957|1=836}})<ref group="Hara" name="Jowa 3"/>, you can see an article about the rank of Junior 1st Rank, 1st Class, Jowa 6th year ({{ill|lt=839|Q23874|qid=Q23874|1=839}}) <ref group="Hara" name="Jowa 6"/>{{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. {{ill|lt=Kaxiang|Q1373157|qid=Q1373157|1=Kashō}}3 years ({{ill|lt=850 years|Q30364|qid=Q30364|1=850}})<ref group="Hara" In name="Kasho 3"/>, Takemiga Mamechi no Mikoto of Kasuga Shrine attained the rank of Shoichii {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}} (there is also a view that Kasuga Shrine, which was the source of the solicitation, was also awarded the rank at the same time<ref name="Kasuga Heibonsha"/>).{{ill|lt=Extension (era name)|Q1327274|qid=Q1327274|lt=Extension|1=Enchō}} "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" established in 5 years ({{ill|lt=927|Q30470|qid=Q30470|1=927}}) Hitachi Kokujo. </ref>In {{ill|lt=Hitachikuni|Q1055353|qid=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}{{ill|lt=Kashima County (Ibaraki Prefecture)|Q6374307|qid=Q6374307|lt=Kashima County|1=Kashima District, Ibaraki}} "Kashima Jingu Meishin University In addition to being listed as "Monthly New Year" and listed at {{ill|UNKNOWN|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikiuchi|1=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} ({{ill|lt=Meishin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964|1=Myōjin Taisha}}), {{ill|lt=Monthly Festival|Q11516161|qid=Q11516161|1=Tsukinami-no-Matsuri}}・{{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}} which was kept in Heihaku during {{ill|lt=Ninamesai|Q11501518|qid=Q11501518|1=Niiname-no-Matsuri}}. In addition, at that time, only three shrines, Dai Jingu ({{ill|lt=Ise Jingu|Q687168|qid=Q687168|1=Ise Grand Shrine}}), Katori Jingu, and Kashima Jingu, were listed with the title ``{{ill|lt=Jingu|Q120680118|qid=Q120680118|1=List of Jingū}}'' in the Shinmeicho.{{Sfn|Seiji Okada|2011}}. Also, in Hitachi Province, it came to be ranked as {{ill|lt=Ichinomiya|Q1656379|qid=Q1656379|1=Ichinomiya}}<ref group="note">The first mention of ``Ichinomiya'' was in 1213 {{Harv|Ichinomiya system|2000|p=230}}. </ref>.

==== From Kamakura period to Edo period ====
Because Kashima Jingu enshrines the god of war, its divine authority was maintained even in the samurai era of {{ill|lt=medieval times|Q12554|qid=Q12554|1=Middle Ages}}, and it was revered by successive samurai governments and daimyo {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Just as many shrine fiefs were donated by {{ill|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800|qid=Q242800|1=Minamoto no Yoritomo}}, it is confirmed that there were many dedications and fief donations from samurai families to the shrine {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. On the other hand, samurai families often advanced into the shrine priesthood and invaded the divine territory.{{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}} link|Ojou clan|Q11435585}} family) was appointed as the Souichi envoy and entered the management of the shrine, which led to them moving away from the influence of the Fujiwara clan.{{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}<ref name="Heibonsha"/>. In the {{ill|lt=Muromachi period|Q334845|qid=Q334845|1=Muromachi period}}, invasions by local forces progressed in parallel with the samurai government's donation of shrines, and it is said that there was no money to build the shrine.{{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Heibonsha)|1982}}.

[[File:The Famous Scenes of the Sixty States 21 Hitachi.jpg|thumb|160px|right|{{center|``Hitachi Kashima Daijingu Shrine''}}{{small|{{ill|lt=Hiroshige Utagawa|Q200798|qid=Q200798|1=Hiroshige}} from ``{{ill|lt=Illustrated Guide to Famous Places in the Sixty-odd States|Q6724086|qid=Q6724086|1=Famous Views of the Sixty-odd Provinces}}''. }}]]In the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, it was revered by the {{ill|lt=Edo shogunate|Q205662|qid=Q205662|1=Tokugawa shogunate}}, and in the 10th year of {{ill|lt=Keicho|Q1328185|qid=Q1328185|1=Keichō}} ({{jal Ink|1605|Q6741}}), the main shrine (currently the shrine building of Setsusha Okumiya) was built by {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|Q171977|qid=Q171977|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}}{{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. {{ill|lt=Motowa (Japan)|Q635245|qid=Q635245|lt=Genna|1=Genna}}5 ({{ill|lt=1619|Q6804|qid=Q6804|1=1619}}), Tokugawa Hidetada built the current shrine building, {{ill|lt=Kanei|Q1192913|qid=Q1192913|1=Kan'ei}}11. ({{ill|lt=1634|Q6872|qid=Q6872|1=1634}}), the tower gate etc. were built by {{ill|lt=Yorifusa Tokugawa|Q1133680|qid=Q1133680|1=Tokugawa Yorifusa}}{{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}.

==== After Meiji ====
After {{ill|lt=Meiji Restoration|Q8707|qid=Q8707|1=Meiji Restoration}}, in {{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}4 ({{ill|lt=1871|Q7746|qid=Q7746|1=1871}}) {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=153}} listed as {{ill|lt=Modern Shrine Ranking System#Kansha|Q712534|comment=this used to link to modern system but that one is too overlinked|lt=Kanpei Taisha|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}} in the Modern Shrine Ranking System|Q712534}}. After the war, it was listed as {{ill|lt=Beppyō Shrine|Q10898274|qid=Q10898274|1=Beppyo shrine}} of {{ill|lt=Shinja Honcho|Q908077|qid=Q908077|1=Association of Shinto Shrines}}.

In {{ill|lt=Showa|Q327567|qid=Q327567|1=Shōwa era}}43 ({{ill|lt=1968|Q2644|qid=Q2644|1=1968}}), the Great Torii (Ninitorii) was rebuilt using granite from Kasama City, Ibaraki Prefecture, to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the Meiji Restoration.<ref name="Tokyo Shimbun"/> In 1986 ({{ill|lt=1986|Q2430|qid=Q2430|1=1986}}), the precincts were designated as a national {{ill|lt=historic site|Q1081138|qid=Q1081138|1=Historic site}}<ref name="historic site"/>.{{ill|lt=Heisei|Q234510|qid=Q234510|1=Heisei era}} Due to the {{ill|lt=Heisei|Q234510|qid=Q234510|1=Heisei era}} {{ill|lt=Tohoku Pacific Coast Earthquake|Q36204|qid=Q36204|1=2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami}} that occurred on March 11, 2011 ({{ill|lt=2011|Q1994|qid=Q1994|1=2011}}) and its aftershocks, the large stone torii gate (second torii gate) The torii gate of Mitarai Pond collapsed, and 64 stone {{ill|lt=lanterns|Q12012294|qid=Q12012294|1=Stone lantern}} in the precincts also collapsed, and the main shrine {{ill|lt=Chigi/Katsunoki|Q87220234|qid=Q87220234|lt=Chigi|1=chigi and katsuogi}} was also damaged, with the total damage amounting to 107 million yen.<ref name="Ibaraki Shimbun">{{Cite news |title=Splendid stillness and movement Next month 1st and 2nd Autumn festival Ancient style and Heian picture scroll|newspaper=Ibaraki Shimbun |date=2013-08-29 |edition=Morning edition |page=16}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|url=http://city.kashima.ibaraki.jp/info/detail.php?no=5792|title=2011.3.11 Records of the Great East Japan Earthquake|publisher=Kashima City|date=2012-6 |page=3 |accessdate=2014-7-23}}</ref>. Afterwards, the Otorii was rebuilt using cedar from the temple grounds, and a completion ceremony was held in June 2014 ({{ill|lt=2014|Q1999|qid=Q1999|1=2014}}).<ref name="Tokyo Shimbun"/>In addition, in 2011, the first large-scale excavation survey was carried out in the precincts in conjunction with the rebuilding of the prayer hall and shrine office on the northwest side of the precincts. At this time, in addition to remains and artifacts related to blacksmithing dating back to the Nara period, it was found that the land had been leveled many times over the years.{{Sfn|2012 Excavation Survey Report}}As part of the major renovations for Reiwa, renovation work on the main hall of the inner shrine, main hall of the main shrine, and tower gate has been underway since {{ill|lt=2021|Q49628|qid=Q49628|1=2021}} (Reiwa 3), and is scheduled to be completed in {{ill|lt=2026|Q49613|qid=Q49613|1=2026}}.<ref name="tokyo-np20231028">{{Cite web|Japanese book|url=https://www.tokyo-np.co.jp/article/286516|title=Kashima Jingu Shrine's curvaceous cypress bark roof has been restored. 170,000 pieces of roofing have been replaced. Work on the main shrine's Heideno Worship Hall is completed in November. Visitors can now visit in December.|publisher=Tokyo Shimbun|accessdate=2023-10-31}}</ref>. Construction of Okumiya will start and be completed in February 2021<ref>{{Cite web|Japanese book|url=https://www.tokyo-np.co.jp/article/135825|title=Kashima Jingu "Okumiya" unveiled for the first time - Ieyasu dedication "cypress bark roofing" coming soon |publisher=Tokyo Shimbun|accessdate=2023-10-31}}</ref>, construction of the Main Shrine Heiden Hall of Worship will begin in 2022 and be completed in November 2023.<ref> name="tokyo-np20231028" />. Construction of the tower gate is scheduled to begin in 2024, with major renovations to be completed in 2026.<ref name="tokyo-np20231028" />

In the later ``{{ill|lt=Nihon Sandai Jirroku|Q1052981|qid=Q1052981|1=Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku}}'', these three Kanjomotosha were promoted following the strategy in this article, so it is thought that Motosha and Kasugasha were promoted at the same time. </ref>. }}

</div>“Hitachi Province Fudoki” <ref group="Hara" As seen in name="Fudoki"/>, many {{ill|lt=Nakatomi clan|Q1198447|qid=Q1198447|lt=Nakatomibe|1=Nakatomi clan}} and {{ill|lt=Urabe clan|Q11409028|qid=Q11409028|lt=Urabe|1=Urabe clan}} lived in ancient Hitachi, and it is said that many of them also served as Shinto priests {{Sfn|Kashima clan (national history)|1983}}. Tenpyo 18 ({{ill|lt=746|Q23616|qid=Q23616|1=746}}) <ref group="Hara"> Shoku Nihongi, March 24th, Tenpyo 18 (746) (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). According to </ref>, the surname ``Nakatomi Kashima{{ill|lt=ren|Q2735611|qid=Q2735611|1=Muraji}}'' was given to Nakatomibe 20 and Urabe 5, who lived in the area {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. From then on, the main priests at the shrine were the ``Nakatomi Kashima clan'' (Nakatomi clan) in this area and the ``''{{ill|lt=Onakatomi clan|Q11431853|qid=Q11431853|1=Ōnakatomi clan}}'' in the center. Regarding the office structure, ``{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}'' was established in 5 years ({{ill|lt=927|Q30470|qid=Q30470|1=927}}) <ref group="hara">``Engishiki'' Volume 15, Kashima Katori-jo (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref><ref group="Hara">"Engishiki" Volume 3 Extraordinary Festival Jinguji Kirokujo (Refer to {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). According to </ref>, the official structure of the shrine is made up of one chief priest, one Negi, one Yuki, and one Moni, and that the chief priest is equivalent to the rank of Jūhachii {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}.In the {{ill|lt=Kamakura period|Q236205|qid=Q236205|1=Kamakura period}}, the Hitachi {{jalink|Ojo clan|Q1 The {{ill|lt=Kashima clan|Q11677139|qid=Q11677139|1=Kashima clan}} of the 1435585}} family was appointed to the Sodai Event {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Kadokawa)|1983}}. Until then, the Fujiwara clan had basically held the right to appoint Shinto priests, but with the advancement of this samurai family, they were no longer under the influence of the Fujiwara clan {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Kadokawa)|1983}}.

According to the "Record of the Appointment of Various Priests" written in {{ill|lt=Bun'ei|Q1010103|qid=Q1010103|1=Bun'ei}} 3rd year ({{ill|lt=1266|Q5517|qid=Q5517|1=1266}}), the priesthood of the shrine at that time included the chief priest, Omineyoshi, Monoki, his father (Chitomi Neyoshi), and So. It is said that there were easily more than 50 people at the grand event, including the Kenbishi, the Sorei, the Oshiryo, the Miyasuke, Goneyoshi, Wada, Gonnobu, Masuda, Soshin and Tadokoro, the three organizers, the Shinto priest, the head of the town, the magistrate, etc.{{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Kadokawa)|1983}}.

The main positions are as follows.

; Daiguji
: "Daiguuji". The chief executive of the shrine {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=205}}.: In the old days, the position was filled by the central {{ill|lt=Onakatomi clan|Q11431853|qid=Q11431853|1=Ōnakatomi clan}}, but from the {{ill|lt=Nagamoto|Q1193557|qid=Q1193557|1=Chōgen}} years ({{ill|lt=1028|Q19273|qid=Q19273|1=1028}}-{{ill|lt=1037|Q19335|qid=Q19335|1=1037}}), the Onakatomi clan and the Nakatomi clan (Nakatomi Kashima clan) ) began to serve alternately, and after the {{ill|lt=Kencho|Q1194270|qid=Q1194270|1=Kenchō}} years ({{ill|lt=1249|Q5485|qid=Q5485|1=1249}}-{{ill|lt=1256|Q5502|qid=Q5502|1=1256}}), the Nakatomi clan succeeded (called the Hanawa clan in early modern times) {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}.
; Omineyoshi
: "Onion". He carried out general affairs, and also performed deity offerings and offerings {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=205}}.
: Negi was confirmed in the 8th year of Jogan (866), and the Joan era ({{ill|lt=1171|Q19685|qid=Q19685|1=1171}}-{{ill|lt=1175|Q19692|qid=Q19692|1=1175}}) was the beginning of Onegi, and thereafter the Nakatomi clan was hereditary (called the Hanyu clan in early modern times) {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. At one time, the Kashima clan (Hitachi Daijo clan) was also in charge {{Sfn|Kashima clan (national history)|1983}}.
: Since the Middle Ages, he had more fiefs than the Grand Shrine, and was practically the most powerful in the shrine {{Sfn|Sharyo (National History)|1983}}.
; remembrance
: "Monoimi". Main shrine inner servant {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=205}}.: In ancient times, the unmarried daughters of Shinto priests were selected, and from the end of the Middle Ages, the women of Toneyoshi (also known as Sentomi Neyoshi and Monokiyo) were chosen {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Toneyoshi (Monoki's father) was originally a member of the Nakatomi clan, but at the end of the Middle Ages, the Higashi clan of the {{ill|lt=Chiba clan|Q2975237|qid=Q2975237|1=Chiba clan}} school succeeded him and played an important role as Monoki's guardian {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}.
: Moni is an entity that should not be seen by the public, and among the many festivals at the shrine, it is said that he only appeared six times a year: the Hongu Festival (door-opening ritual), the Okumiya Festival, the Yabusame Festival, the Omiya Festival, the Shogun Festival, and the {{ill|lt=Ouse Shrine|Q17221225|qid=Q17221225|lt=Ouse Shrine|1=Ōu Shrine}} Festival.{{Sfn|Ouse Shrine (Gods)|1984}}. It is said that the first Moni was Amakurame, the daughter of {{ill|lt=Empress Jingu|Q232803|qid=Q232803|1=Empress Jingū}} {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=94}}, and because she held the position for life, there were only 27 people in total by the time of its abolition in the Meiji period {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Shikiuchisha)|1976}}. Monoi Miyakata, where Monoi once resided, is said to be next to the shrine shrine (Kyogaisesusha) {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}.

=== Company territory ===
"{{ill|lt=Hitachikuni Fudoki|Q11481687|qid=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}" <ref group="Hara" name="Fudoki"/> and "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" <ref name="Shikibujo" group="Hara">"Engishiki" Volume 18 Shikibujo Gunji-jo (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). According to </ref>, {{ill|lt=Hitachi Province|Q1055353|qid=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}{{ill|lt=Kashima County (Ibaraki Prefecture)|Q6374307|qid=Q6374307|lt=Kashima County|1=Kashima District, Ibaraki}}, where the Jingu is located, was {{ill|lt=Kamigun|Q11590937|qid=Q11590937|1=Kamigun}}, that is, the entire county was designated as the sacred territory of the Jingu.

In addition, in "Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki" <ref group="Hara" name="Fudoki"/>, there is the following description of {{ill|lt=Kobe (Minbe)|Q11589711|qid=Q11589711|lt=Kobe|1=Kanbe (social class)}}, that is, the attached private house for maintaining rituals {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}.
* Before {{ill|lt=Emperor Kotoku|Q317980|qid=Q317980|1=Emperor Kōtoku}}, 8 houses
* Emperor Kotoku year ({{ill|lt=645|Q31040|qid=Q31040|1=645}}-{{ill|lt=654|Q31109|qid=Q31109|1=654}}), an increase of 50 houses (total of 58 houses)
* {{ill|lt=Emperor Tenmu|Q335181|qid=Q335181|1=Emperor Tenmu}} ({{ill|lt=673|Q31105|qid=Q31105|1=673}}-{{ill|lt=686|Q30619|qid=Q30619|1=686}}), an increase of 9 units (total of 67 units)* {{ill|lt=Emperor Jito|Q232026|qid=Q232026|1=Empress Jitō}} 4th year ({{ill|lt=690|Q23472|qid=Q23472|1=690}}), decrease by 2 houses (total 65 houses) - This seems to be the influence of the creation of "{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kotora Nenshi|1=UNKNOWN}}" {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}.

Later, in a document from the {{ill|lt=Nara period|Q189178|qid=Q189178|1=Nara period}}, there is the following entry:{{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}{{Sfn|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}.
* In {{ill|lt=Tenpyo Houji|Q1346307|qid=Q1346307|1=Tenpyō-hōji}} 2nd year ({{ill|lt=758 years|Q30538|qid=Q30538|1=758}}), 218 people were named Kobe ("Shoku Nihongi") <ref group="Hara">Shoku Nihongi, Tenpyoji 2nd year (758), September Choushi (8th) article (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref>
* In the first year of {{ill|lt=Tenpyo Jingo|Q1373181|qid=Q1373181|1=Tenpyō-jingo}} ({{ill|lt=765|Q31216|qid=Q31216|1=765}}), Kashima Shrine donated 20 houses in Kobe to Kasuga Shrine ("{{ill|lt=Shinsho Kakuchofusho|Q11502312|qid=Q11502312|1=Shinshō Kyakuchokufushō}}") <ref name="Shinsho" group="Hara"/>
* In the first year of {{ill|lt=Jingo Keiun|Q1373049|qid=Q1373049|1=Jingo-keiun}} ({{ill|lt=767|Q30561|qid=Q30561|1=AD 767}}), 80 male and 75 female Shinsen were incorporated into Ryomin ("Shoku Nihongi") <ref group="Hara">Shoku Nihongi, Jingo Keiun 1st year (767) April Koushi (21st) article (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref>* {{ill|lt=Hoki|Q18520676|qid=Q18520676|1=Hōki}}4th year ({{ill|lt=773|Q31131|qid=Q31131|1=773}}), marriages between 105 Shinsen and good people are prohibited (Shoku Nihongi) <ref group="Hara">Shoku Nihongi, June 2nd, Hoki 4th year (773), article (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref>
* In the 11th year of Houki ({{ill|lt=780|Q30519|qid=Q30519|1=780}}), the incorporation of 774 missing Shinsen into Kobe was approved, and the Shinto priests were prohibited from using good people as Shinshin (Shoku Nihongi) <ref group="Hara">Shoku Nihongi, December 22nd, Hoki 11th year (780), article (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref>
* {{ill|lt=Enryaku|Q1373176|qid=Q1373176|1=Enryaku}} 1st year ({{ill|lt=782|Q30550|qid=Q30550|1=782}}), 2 Kobes in Mutsu Province ("Shinsho Kakuchofusho") <ref name="Shinsho" group="Hara"/>
* 5th year of Enryaku ({{ill|lt=786|Q30307|qid=Q30307|1=786}}), 105 people in Kobe, 50 people in Kamzebe, 685 people in the division, 2,676 people in the non-class ("Shinsho Kokucho Fusho") Daido 1st year (806) (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref>

In the {{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292|1=Heian period}}, it is said that the head of the Fuji clan donated 10 houses from his official servant as an example {{Sfn|sharyo (national history)|1983}}. From the end of the Heian period onwards, each priest inherited the fiefs and private fiefs attached to them {{Sfn|sharyo (national history)|1983}}.In the Middle Ages, there were frequent encroachments on the shrine's territory, and it is said that there was not enough money to build the shrine.{{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Later, the encroachment was stopped by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and in {{ill|lt=Bunroku|Q1373039|qid=Q1373039|1=Bunroku}}4 ({{ill|lt=1595|Q6782|qid=Q6782|1=1595}}), the shrine territory was determined to be 405 koku {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}.

Tokugawa Ieyasu added 1,500 koku in {{ill|lt=Keicho|Q1328185|qid=Q1328185|1=Keichō}} 7th year ({{ill|lt=1602|Q6727|qid=Q6727|1=1602}}), and the shrine territory became 2,000 koku. (including 100 koku for Daiguji, 300 koku for Tonegi, 40 koku each for Ounegi and Daishu) {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}{{Sfn|Sharyo (National History)|1983}}.

=== Shrine building construction ===
Regarding the construction of the shrine building, it can be seen that it was already constructed in the {{ill|lt=Emperor Tenchi|Q314802|qid=Q314802|1=Emperor Tenji}} years ({{ill|lt=668|Q30116|qid=Q30116|1=668}}-{{ill|lt=672|Q30601|qid=Q30601|1=672}}) in the "Hitachi Province Fudoki" <ref group="Hara" name="Fudoki"/>.According to "Kashima Choreki," the Seiden and Temporary Halls were built in the first year of {{ill|lt=Taiho (Japan)|Q1346269|qid=Q1346269|lt=Taiho|1=Taihō (era)}} ({{ill|lt=701|Q23496|qid=Q23496|1=701}}), and from this time it was decided that they would be built once every 20 years {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Kadokawa)|1983}}. When it was built in this year, the current main shrine and {{ill|lt=Okumiya|Q11445659|qid=Q11445659|1=Okumiya}} are said to have been alternately used as the shrine grounds.{{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Shikinai Shrine)|1976}}. The construction details are: {{ill|lt=Konin|Q1373070|qid=Q1373070|1=Kōnin (era)}} 3rd year ({{ill|lt=812th|Q31114|qid=Q31114|1=812}}) <ref group="Hara"> "Nihon Koki" Article on June 5th, 812 (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). In </ref>, the rebuilding of the entire shrine building was changed from rebuilding only the main hall.{{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Kadokawa)|1983}}. After that, there was an article in the 8th year of Jogan ({{ill|lt=866|Q23872|qid=Q23872|1=866}}) in the ``Nihon Sandai Jiroku'' ({{ill|lt=866|Q23872|qid=Q23872|1=866}}), and ``Engishiki'' special festival <ref name="repair" group="hara"> ``Engishiki'' volume 3 temporary festival shrine repair article (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref> shows that it was constructed {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Kadokawa)|1983}}. According to an article in ``Nihon Sandai Jiroku'', it required more than 50,000 branches of lumber, 160,000 ingenious workers, and 180,000 bundles of rice {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (National History)|1983}}.According to the "Kashima Town History", the construction years from the Heian period to the Sengoku period were Jogan 8 (866), {{ill|lt=Tenkei|Q1327340|qid=Q1327340|1=Tengyō}}3 === Precincts ===
The place where the shrine is located is called ``Mikasayama'' (Mikasayama).{{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=80}}. This precinct is designated as a national historic site as it is an important ruin in the history of Japan (also includes the precincts of Sessha Sakado Shrine, the precincts of Sessha Numao Shrine, and the ruins of the Kashima Gun family) <ref name="historic site"/>.

The shrine grounds are approximately 70 hectares in area. </ref>. Approximately 40 hectares of this area is a dense forest of trees, which has been designated as a natural monument by Ibaraki Prefecture as the Kashima Jingu Forest.<ref name="Ibaraki Shimbun"/> Approximately 800 species of plants grow in the forest, and there are many large trees that symbolize the long history of the shrine, making it the largest evergreen evergreen forest in Ibaraki Prefecture.

=== Shrine building ===
[[File:Kashima-jingu honden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Main shrine (National Important Cultural Property)}}{{Small|Ishi-no-ma and Heiden are connected to the front. }}]]
[[File:Kashima-jingu karidono.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Karaden (National Important Cultural Property)}}]]
[[File:Kashima-jingu roumon.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Romon (National Important Cultural Property)}}{{Small|One of Japan's three major tower gates. }}]]The main shrine buildings consist of the main hall, the stone room, the hall of worship, and the hall of worship. Both are from the early {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963|1=Edo period}} {{jalink|Genwa period} (Japan)|Q635245|It was built in 1619|Q6804}} by the order of the second generation of {{ill|lt=Edo Shogunate|Q205662|qid=Q205662|1=Tokugawa shogunate}}, {{ill|lt=Hidetada Tokugawa|Q314464|qid=Q314464|1=Tokugawa Hidetada}}, and by Choji Suzuki, the leader of the shogunate. The Heiden is built behind the Worship Hall, and the main shrine and the Heiden are connected by a corridor called ``Ishi-no-ma'', making it a complex shrine building. Even after entering the tower gate, the approach continues straight to the east, but the shrine building is in a unique position, connecting from the right (south) midway along the approach. For this reason, the shrine building faces north, and this is said to be a layout inspired by Ezo in the north.'''The main shrine'' is a Sangen shrine {{ill|lt=Nagazuzō|Q210684|qid=Q210684|1=Nagare-zukuri}}, with one room of Mukaihai {{ill|lt=cypress bark|Q90373477|qid=Q90373477|1=cypress bark roof}}. <ref name="Main shrine"/> is lacquered with richly colored pillar capitals and fittings. Until construction in 1619, the current Okumiya shrine building was used as the main shrine. The main shrine faces north, but the shrine inside is located at the southwest corner of the inner shrine and should face east, not facing worshipers (see the diagram below), and it has been pointed out that it is related to the {{ill|lt=Izumo Taisha|Q696362|qid=Q696362|1=Izumo-taisha}} main shrine.{{Sfn |Tomomi|2000|p=27}} (However, in the main shrine where the priests and others entered, there are many cases where the building is oriented sideways when viewed from the front, following the example of ancient palaces.<ref>{{ill|lt=Masayuki Miura|Q11356475|qid=Q11356475|1=Masayuki Miura}} “The Main Hall of a Shrine: The Space of God in Architecture,” Yoshikawa Kobunkan, 2013, pp. 182-189. According to ``Kashima Shrine Biography'', in ancient times the main shrine was described as ``Akazu no Goten,'' which was not usually opened, and the doors were opened only on January 7th of each year to exchange coins.{{Sfn|Kashima Moni (National History)|1983}} Behind this main shrine stands a gigantic cedar tree {{ill|lt=sacred tree|Q48743901|qid=Q48743901|1=Shinboku}}, which is 43 meters tall and 12 meters around its roots and is said to be approximately 1,000 years old. Further back, through the Tamagaki fence, there is a stone with a diameter of about 80 centimeters called ``Kagami-ishi,'' and it is said to be the place where the shrine was founded {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Heibonsha)|1982}}.'''Ishi no Ma'''' has two girders, one beam, and one story, {{ill|lt=gable|Q13308575|qid=Q13308575|1=Kirizuma-style}}, cypress bark roofing, and the front is connected to the hall. Like the main shrine, it is lacquered in rich colors. The ``Hideden'' is a single-story building with two girders and one beam, gabled construction, and a cypress bark roof, and the front is connected to the worship hall. ``The Worship Hall'' is a single-story building with 5-ken rows of girders, 3-room beams, a gabled structure, 1-room facing worship, and a cypress bark roof. Unlike the main shrine and stone room, the Heiden and Worship Hall have a simple design of plain wood, without lacquer or bright colors. These main shrines, stone rooms, shrine halls, and worship halls are designated as important cultural properties of the country <ref name="honden"/>.

A ``karido'' (temporary hall) is built in front of the right front of the worship hall, facing south. Kariden is also written as ``Gonden,'' and is a shrine building used to temporarily enshrine divine spirits during the construction of the main shrine. This temporary shrine was built by Choji Suzuki, the shogunate's chief architect, when the current main shrine was constructed in 1619. The structure is three-span girders, two-span beams, single-story, gabled, one-span, with cypress bark roofing. Since it is a temporary hall, it is relatively simple in construction, but some parts are decorated with lacquer. It is said that when it was first constructed, it was located at the front left of the worship hall, facing west, but after changing its location several times, it was settled on its current location in 1951 ({{ill|lt=1951|Q18591|qid=Q18591|1=1951}}). This temporary hall has been designated as an important cultural property of the country <ref name="Kariden"/>.On the approach to the shrine grounds, there is a ``romon'' facing west, which is counted as one of the ``Three Great Romon Gates of Japan'' <ref name="Sandai Romon" group="Note">"Japan's three major tower gates" include Kashima Shrine and {{ill|lt=Aso Shrine|Q715639|qid=Q715639|1=Aso Shrine}} ({{ill|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture|Q130308|qid=Q130308|1=Kumamoto Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Aso City|Q733681|qid=Q733681|1=Aso, Kumamoto}}), is said to be the tower gate of {{ill|lt=Hakozaki Shrine|Q714742|qid=Q714742|1=Hakozaki Shrine}} ({{ill|lt=Fukuoka Prefecture|Q123258|qid=Q123258|1=Fukuoka Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Fukuoka City|Q26600|qid=Q26600|1=Fukuoka}}). </ref>. It was built in 11 ({{ill|lt=1634|Q6872|qid=Q6872|1=1634}}) by order of {{ill|lt=Yorifusa Tokugawa|Q1133680|qid=Q1133680|1=Tokugawa Yorifusa}}, the first {{ill|lt=Mito domain|Q1146904|qid=Q1146904|lt=Lord of Mito domain|1=Mito Domain}}, and the master carpenter was Yoshimasa Sakagami, an Echizen carpenter. The structure is a two-story building with three rooms and one door (the door is omitted) with a gabled roof.Currently, the roof is made of copper sheets, but it is said that the roof was originally made of cypress bark. It is entirely painted in vermilion lacquer, and the design is modest, with only a small amount of color applied to the transoms. The plaque ``Kashima Torii'' is written by {{ill|lt=Heihachiro Togo|Q296785|qid=Q296785|1=Tōgō Heihachirō}}. The corridors on the left and right sides of the tower gate were created at the same time as the tower gate, but a temple was added later. This tower gate has been designated as a national important cultural property, and the corridor has been designated as a cultural property designated by Kashima City <ref name="Romon"/>.The ''Otorii'' at the entrance to the shrine grounds is made of four cedar trees and measures 10.2 meters in height and 14.6 meters in width. Originally, it was a stone torii made of granite from Kasama City, but it collapsed from the base due to the {{ill|lt=Tohoku Pacific Coast Earthquake|Q36204|qid=Q36204|1=2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami}} that occurred on March 11, 2011 ({{ill|lt=2011|Q1994|qid=Q1994|1=2011}}) and its aftershocks. In response to this, four giant cedar trees were cut down from the grounds of the shrine and it was rebuilt, making it the 11th time since 1664, when records remain. The great torii is characterized by having a log-shaped Kasagi placed on top of two circular pillars, with only the corner being square and protruding outside the pillars.This form is called the ``''Kashima Torii''''<ref>{{Cite web|Japanese book|title=Kashima Torii |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E9%B9%BF%E5%B3%B6%E9%B3%A5%E5%B1%85-462179 |work=Digital Daijisen |accessdate=2014-07-23}}</ref>. The cedar trees used are approximately 500 years old for the left and right pillars, approximately 600 years old for the Kasagi, and approximately 250 years old for the Nuki. The stone from the collapsed torii gate is used for the base of the pillar, called kamebaraishi. |date=2014-06-01 |edition=Morning edition Ibaraki edition |page=24}}</ref>{{Sfn|Notice of Otorii completion festival (Kashima Jingu official website)}}.<gallery>
File:Kashima-jingu haiden-2.JPG|Full view of the shrine<br />{{Small|There is a sacred tree behind the main shrine. }}
File:Kashima Jingu Main Hall Inner Hall.png|Main Hall Floor Plan
</gallery>

=== Keystone ===
[[File:Kashima-jingu kanameishi-1.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|{{ill|lt=Keystone|Q11630053|qid=Q11630053|1=Kaname-ishi}}}}]]
[[File:Kashima-jingu kanameishi-2.JPG|thumb|150px|right|{{Center|Shape of keystone}}]]
'''{{ill|lt=Keystone|Q11630053|qid=Q11630053|1=Kaname-ishi}}''' (Kanameishi) is a spiritual stone located in the eastern part of the temple grounds. {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Heibonsha)|1982}}, also known as ``Mimaishi'' or ``Mountain Palace'' since ancient times. On the ground, it is about 30 cm in diameter and 7 cm in height, and has a concave shape {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=191}}.In the past, it was believed that earthquakes were caused by {{ill|lt=large catfish|Q257275|qid=Q257275|1=Namazu}} (catfish) living underground, so the keystone was worshiped as a guardian deity from earthquakes that suppressed the large catfish.{{Sfn|Keystone (Kashima Shrine) Official website)}}<ref>{{Citation|url=http://www.bousai.go.jp/kyoiku/kyokun/kyoukunnokeishou/rep/1855-ansei-edoJISHIN/index.html|contribution=Chapter 3 Earthquakes and people's imagination|title=Report of the expert committee on the inheritance of disaster lessons|author=Yasunari Abe|editor=Central Disaster Prevention Council Expert Committee on Passing Down Disaster Lessons |publisher=Cabinet Office|date=2004-3 |page=135 |accessdate=2014-7-23}}</ref>. The keystone is said to be a stake that holds the head and tail of a large catfish in place, and although it looks small, it is said that the underground part is large and can never be removed.{{Sfn|Keystone (Kashima Shrine official website)}} According to the "Mito Komon Nintokuroku", the lord of Mito domain {{ill|lt=Mitsukuni|Tokugawa|qid=Tokugawa|ltq=Q1194944}} ordered people to dig around the keystone for 7 days and 7 nights, but the hole returned to its original size the next morning and could not reach the root {{Sfn|Keystone (Kashima Shrine official website)}}. In the past, some of the large earthquakes that occurred in {{ill|lt=Kannazuki|Q6364021|qid=Q6364021|1=Kannazuki}} were caused by Kashimakami going to {{ill|lt=Izumo|Q11395836|qid=Q11395836|1=Izumo}} while he was away. There is also a legend that it occurred because of <ref>{{ill|lt=Tatsuhiko Shibusawa|Q2278628|qid=Q2278628|1=Tatsuhiko Shibusawa}} "Fantastic Zoology" (included in "Golden Age", Rosicrucian Society, July 1971). </ref>.In addition, there is a convex keystone at {{ill|lt=Katori Shrine|Q372380|qid=Q372380|1=Katori Jingū}}, and a similar story is told <ref>Katori Jingu Shrine Edited by Shinshu Katori Jingu Short History (Katori Jingu Shrine Office, 1995) p. 63. </ref>. This keystone is counted as one of the "{{ill|lt=#Kashima Seven Wonders|UNKNOWN|lt=Kashima Seven Wonders}}" {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=191}}.

Regarding Kashima Jingu Shrine and earthquakes, the following earthquake song is known to have been written in the "Ise Calendar" of 9th year ({{ill|lt=1198|Q19750|qid=Q19750|1=1198}}) and appears to be unknown.{{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=18}}
{{Cquote|As long as there is no God of Kashima, a keystone that is loose and slips out|20px|}}

Also, in the first year of {{ill|lt=Yasumoto|Q1194242|qid=Q1194242|1=Kōgen}} ({{ill|lt=1256|Q5502|qid=Q5502|1=1256}}), Mitsutoshi Fujiwara ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Mitsutoshi Hamuro|1=UNKNOWN}}) visited a shrine, he used the keystone as the ``Stone Throne'' and sang the following song.{{Sfn|Jingu Magazine|2004|p=19}}
{{Cquote|I wonder if I'll be able to find it today? Chihayaburu: The stone shrine deep in the mountains|20px|}}

=== Mitarai Pond ===
[[File:Kashima-jingu mitarai.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Mitarai Pond}}]]
``Mitarashike'' (Mitarashike) is a divine pond located in the eastern part of the shrine grounds. The land of Keisai ({{ill|lt=purification|Q1936265|qid=Q1936265|1=Misogi}}) {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=191}}. In ancient times, it is believed that people would take a boat from Ofunazu, where the first torii gate is located, to this place, perform a ritual and then visit the shrine {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Heibonsha)|1982}}, and the pond name ``Mitarai'' is also said to have come from this {{Sfn|Higashimi|2000|p=191}}.

Spring water flows into the pond from the south cliff, and although the water is about 1 meter deep, it is extremely clear {{Sfn|Higashimi|2000|p=21}}. It is said that even if adults or children enter this pond, the depth of the water will not exceed the depth of the water, and it is counted as one of the ``{{ill|lt=#Kashima Seven Wonders|UNKNOWN|lt=Kashima Seven Wonders}}'' {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=191}}.

=== Deer Park ===
There is a deer park within the shrine grounds, where over 30 {{ill|lt=sika deer|Q190516|qid=Q190516|lt=Japanese deer|1=Sika deer}}, {{ill|lt=divine messengers|Q10444973|qid=Q10444973|1=Shinshi}} (messengers of the gods), are kept {{Sfn|deer park (Kashima Shrine official website)}}. Until around the beginning of the Meiji era, many deer were kept as "sacred deer" in deer gardens, similar to Nara's {{ill|lt=Kasuga Taisha|Q714559|qid=Q714559|1=Kasuga-taisha}}<ref>[https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/963454 "Nara and Deer"] Saburo Hatta, Kanpei Taisha Kasuga Shrine Kasuga Deer Conservation Society, Taisho 9, p34</ref>.According to the Kojiki, it was {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ame-kaku-kami|1=UNKNOWN}} (Ame-kaku-kami) who conveyed the life of {{ill|lt=Amaterasu Omikami|Q455602|qid=Q455602|1=Amaterasu}} to Takemikazuchi. {{Sfn|Shikaen (Kashima Shrine official website)}}<ref name="insight">[https://kashimajingu.jp/guidance/%e5%a2%83%e5%86%85%e6%a1%88%e5%86%85/ Kashima Jingu official website precincts guide]</ref>. This "kaku" is said to be "kako", a god derived from deer <ref>[https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%A4%A9%E8%BF%A6%E4%B9%85%E7%A5%9E-1050873 ``Digital version Japanese name encyclopedia +Plus'' Tenkakyujin section] (from Kotobank <Asahi Shimbun>). </ref>Based on this, it is said that deer are used as messengers at the shrine {{Sfn|Deer Park (Kashima Shrine official website)}}. Also, the reason why the name of the shrine changed from ``Koshima'' to ``Kashima'' is said to have come from the deer that was the messenger of the gods. When {{ill|lt=Kasuga Taisha|Q714559|qid=Q714559|1=Kasuga-taisha}} was founded, in the first year of {{ill|lt=Jingo Keiun|Q1373049|qid=Q1373049|1=Jingo-keiun}} ({{ill|lt=767|Q30561|qid=Q30561|1=AD 767}}), a spirit was mounted on the back of a white sacred deer and a large number of deer were taken with it and they set out.<ref name="insight"/>, and is said to have traveled to Nara for a year, and {{ill|lt=Nara no Deer|Q48745785|qid=Q48745785|1=deer in Nara}} is said to have originated from Kashima Shrine {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|pp=147-149}}. This view of Kashima Tate is also known from {{ill|lt=Kasuga Mandara|Q11513629|qid=Q11513629|1=Kasuga Mandalas}}'s ``Shadow of the Kashima Tate Gods'' {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=149}}.<gallery>

File:Kasuga Deities Departing from Kashima Shrine (Kasuga Taisha).jpg|Kashima Shrine Shadows<br />(Kasuga Taisha Shrine collection)
</gallery>

=== Approach ===
[[File:Kashima Shrine 29.jpg|thumb|210px|right|{{Center|West Ichino Torii (Ofunazu, Kashima City)}}{{Small|[[Kasumigaura|Wani River]] ({{ill|lt=Kasumigaura|Q1077984|qid=Q1077984|lt=Kitaura|1=Lake Kasumigaura}}) riverside. }}]]There used to be four Ichi-no-Torii gates at Kashima Shrine, located in the north, south, east, and west, but currently there are three torii gates in the east, west, and south. The first torii gate in the west is located in Ofunazu, Kashima City, on the shore of Lake {{ill|lt=Kitaura|Q11402369|qid=Q11402369|1=Kitaura}}, inside {{ill|lt=Kasumigaura|Q1077984|qid=Q1077984|lt=Wani River|1=Lake Kasumigaura}} ({{Coord|3 5|57|40.01|N|140|36|41.31|E|region:JP-08_type:landmark|name=Ichino Torii (West)}}) {{Sfn|Ichino Torii (Kashima Shrine) Official website)}}. Since Ofunazu has long been a dock for pilgrims visiting the shrine, <ref> "Place Names of Ibaraki Prefecture" (Heibonsha), Ofunatsu Village section. </ref>The shrine town also extends to the west of here. Before these towns were formed in the Middle Ages, it is believed that people took boats from Tsu Tozai Shrine in Ofunatsu to Mitarai Pond, where they made a cleansing ritual and visited the shrine {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Heibonsha)|1982}}. The current torii was rebuilt in June 2013, and had been moved from the water to land during the Showa period due to embankment construction, but was rebuilt on the water for the Mifune Festival in 2014. This torii gate is large-scale, measuring 18.5 meters high from the riverbed and 22.5 meters wide, making it one of the largest floating torii gates in Japan. During the Mifune Festival, the gozabune depart from here.The East Ichi-no-Torii Gate is located on Akashi Beach facing the {{ill|lt=Pacific Ocean|Q98|qid=Q98|1=Pacific Ocean}} ({{Coord|35|59|43.34|N|140|39|22.91|E|region:JP-08_type:landmark|name=Ichi-no-Torii (East)}}) {{Sfn|Ichi-no-Torii (Kashima Shrine official website)}}. According to legend, Takematsuchi and Tsunetsunushi landed on Akashi Beach, and Tsunetsushi moved from Numao to Katori, where he was desired, and Takemitsuchi moved from Numao to the current main shrine.{{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=53-54}}In addition, the Minami Ichi-no-Torii gate used to be located in Hikawa, Kamisu City, but now the Ichi-no-Torii gate of {{ill|lt=Ikusu Shrine|Q11073095|qid=Q11073095|1=Ikisu Shrine}} has been used instead ({{Coord|35|53|5.94 |N | 140 Official website)}}. The first torii gate in the north was located in Kobehara, but it has long since been lost. Official website)}}, newly built in front of Togakushi Shrine (Hamatsuga, Kashima City) in 2017 ({{Coord|36|3|11.76|N|140|36|25.25|E|region:JP-08_ type:landmark|name=Ichi-no-Torii (North)}}）<ref>[http://ibarakinews.jp/news/newsdetail.php?f_jun=15068695163300 "'Kita Ichino Torii' completed; east, west, north, south, and north of Kashima Jingu Shrine completed" (Ibaraki Shimbun, October 2, 2017 article).</ref>.

=== Setsusha ===
There are 23 shrines in total: 7 shrines (3 inside the precincts, 4 outside the shrine grounds), 15 shrines (8 shrines inside the shrine grounds, 7 outside the shrine grounds), and 1 shrine under its jurisdiction (1 shrine inside the shrine grounds).<ref>Setsume shrines are based on Chapter 3 (pp. 52-68) of the New Kashima Jingu Journal. </ref>.

=== Sessha ===
{{List of coordinates|Section=Setsusha}}
[[File:Kashima-jingu Okumiya.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Okumiya (National Important Cultural Property)}}]]
'''Okumiya''
:* Deity enshrined: Takemikazuchi Okami {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Aratama|1=UNKNOWN}}
: "Okunomiya". Further down the approach from the main shrine building is the Precinct Setsusha ({{Coord|35|58|12.57|N|140|38|06.79|E|region:JP-08_type:landmark|name=Precinct Setsusha: Okumiya}}), which faces north like the main shrine. "{{ill|lt=Azuma Kagami|Q1042324|qid=Q1042324|1=Azuma Kagami}}" <ref group="Hara">"Azuma Kagami" Article dated February 12, 1241. In </ref>, there is a record that in the fire of {{ill|lt=Ninji|Q1194262|qid=Q1194262|1=Ninji}} 2nd year ({{ill|lt=1241|Q5436|qid=Q5436|1=1241}}), ``the back palace of the unopened palace was not burnt down.'' ``Zuno Goten'' refers to the main shrine, and ``Okugoten'' refers to the inner shrine, and it is thought that the inner shrine already existed in the Kamakura period.: The current shrine building is the former main hall of the main shrine built by {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|Q171977|qid=Q171977|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} in {{ill|lt=Keicho|Q1328185|qid=Q1328185|1=Keichō}}10 ({{ill|lt=1605|Q6741|qid=Q6741|1=1605}}) as a thank you for the {{ill|lt=Battle of Sekigahara|Q234188|qid=Q234188|lt=Sekigahara|1=Battle of Sekigahara}} victory in the early Edo period.<ref name="Okumiya"/>. During the reconstruction in 1619, it was moved to its current location and became the main hall of the Okumiya <ref name="Okumiya"/>. The structure is built in the style of Sangensha and has a one-room front shrine, but it is thought that it was later remodeled to model the current main shrine during repairs. Although it has a simple design made entirely of plain wood, the carvings also show the bold spirit of the Momoyama period. <ref name="Okumiya"/> is the oldest shrine within the shrine grounds and has been designated as a national important cultural property.

[[File:Kashima-jingu Takafusasha.JPG|thumb|170px|right|{{Center|Takafusa Shrine}}]]
; Takafusa Shrine
:* Deity enshrined: {{ill|lt=Tatehazuchi God|Q10940642|qid=Q10940642|lt=Tatehazuchi God|1=Takehazuchi}}
: "Takafusa Jinja". Precinct Setsusha ({{Coord|35|58|09.12|N|140|37|53.29|E|region:JP-08_type:landmark|name=Precinct Setsusha: Takafusa Shrine}}) is located in front of the main shrine building. It is traditional practice to visit the shrine before visiting the main shrine {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=57}}.: According to "Nihon Shoki," the enshrined deity was dispatched by Takemiko Tsuchi no Kami and played an active role in the subjugation of {{ill|lt=Amatsu Monsei|Q4740636|qid=Q4740636|lt=Amagokakoseio|1=Amatsu-Mikaboshi}}, and is enshrined as the main enshrined deity at {{ill|lt=Shizu Shrine|Q11663648|qid=Q11663648|1=Shizu Shrine}} (Ninomiya, Hitachi Province).
: It is said that the current shrine building was built in 1619 when the main shrine was rebuilt.{{Sfn|Jingu Shi|2004|p=57}}. This shrine is considered to be one of the oldest among the shrines due to its enshrined location and the relationship with the deity enshrined {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=58}}.

The origin of Mikasa Shrine, including the deity it enshrines, is unknown since ancient times {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=58}}. On the shrine side, since the area is called ``Mt. Mikasa,'' it is assumed that he is the god of the landowner.{{Sfn|Jingu Magazine|2004|p=59}} Regarding the name ``Mt. Mikasa'', it has been pointed out that it is related to {{ill|lt=Mt. Kasuga (Nara Prefecture)|Q11513602|qid=Q11513602|lt=Mt. Mikasa|1=Mount Kasuga}} (Mt. Mt. Mt. Mikasa) in Nara {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=59}}.[[File:Ato-no-miya (Kashima-jingu sessha) -1.JPG|thumb|170px|right|{{Center|Ato-no-miya (Kashima-shi Jinno)}}]]
