: "Ato no Miya". Kyoto Gaisetsusha. The company name is also called ``Ara Matsuri Shrine''. In ancient times, the enshrined deity was Omagatsu no Mikoto {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Gods)|1984}}. It is said to be the first place of descent of the Kashima god, and it is said that the god Takemikazuchi departed from here when praying for Kasuga, Nara {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=59}}. There used to be a ``Monomiyakata'' next to the ruins of the shrine, where the female priest (moni) who was in charge of the shrine's rituals lived.

[[File:Sakato-jinja (Kashima-jingu sessha) -1.JPG|thumb|170px|right|{{Center|Sakado Shrine<br />(Yamanoue, Kashima City)}}]]
; Sakado Shrine
:* Enshrined place: Yamanokami, Kashima City ({{Coord|35|59|12.87|N|140|37|32.46|E|region:JP-08_type:landmark|name=Gaito-setsusha: Sakado Shrine}})
:* Enshrined deity: {{ill|lt=Amagiya Mikoto|Q2564508|qid=Q2564508|1=Ame-no-Koyane}}: "Sakato Jinja". Kyoto Gaisetsusha. In "Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki" <ref group="Hara" name="Fudoki"/>, it appears that the main shrine, Numao Shrine, and Sakado Shrine were collectively called ``Koshima Tendaijin'' {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Heibonsha)|1982}}. The enshrined deity is the ancestral deity of Onakatomi Jinmonkatsu no Mikoto, who is mentioned in ``Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki,'' and is the guardian deity of {{ill|lt=Nakatomi clan|Q1198447|qid=Q1198447|1=Nakatomi clan}} and {{ill|lt=Fujiwara clan|Q641628|qid=Q641628|1=Fujiwara clan}}. On the other hand, {{jalink|Nukatabe clan|Q5 is the outside ancestor of Nao Asuka and the Kashima Daiguji family {{ill|lt=Kashima clan|Q11677139|qid=Q11677139|lt=Nakatomi Kashimaren|1=Nakatomi Kashimaren}} 5532736|Nukataberen}}'s founder {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Sakado Biko no Mikoto|1=UNKNOWN}} and <ref>Hisao Hoga "Tribes that worship the god of the seven moons" "Research on ancient clans ⑤ Nakatomi clan Descendants of the Ancient Urami Department Who Responsible for Divination,” Aogaki Publishing, 2014, 138 pages. </ref>There is also a theory that the original enshrined deity is Hosai-kami of {{ill|lt=Nakakunizo|Q11378492|qid=Q11378492|1=Naka no Kuni no Miyatsuko}}, who took control of the area with the backing of the royal power in the first half of the 6th century.<ref>Yoshinobu Kimoto, Kodai Shironju (Iwata Shoin, 2020)</ref>.
: The main shrine is flat, and the worship hall is gable.{{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=55}}. The shrine building faces east, and it has been pointed out that Sakado Shrine is directly opposite the first torii gate in the east (Akashi no Hama) {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Gods)|1984}}. The grounds of Sakado Shrine are designated as a national historic site (included within the grounds of the main shrine) <ref name="historic site"/>. Additionally, within the grounds of the main shrine there is a place of worship for Sakado Shrine.[[File:Numao-jinja (Kashima-jingu sessha) -2.JPG|thumb|170px|right|{{Center|Numao Shrine (Numao, Kashima City)}}]]
; Numao Shrine
:* Enshrined place: Numao, Kashima City ({{Coord|36|00|03.55|N|140|37|25.17|E|region:JP-08_type:landmark|name=Gaikensha: Numao Shrine}})
:* Deity enshrined: {{ill|lt=Kyotsu no Nushikami|Q1107286|qid=Q1107286|1=Futsunushi}}
: "Numaojinja". Kyoto Gaisetsusha. In "Hitachikuni Fudoki" <ref group="Hara" name="Fudoki"/>, it appears that the three shrines, the main shrine, Sakado Shrine, and Numao Shrine, were collectively called ``Koshima Tendaijin'' {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Heibonsha)|1982}}. The enshrined deity is the main enshrined deity of {{ill|lt=Katori Shrine|Q372380|qid=Q372380|1=Katori Jingū}}, and is said to have founded the eastern region along with Takemikazuchi no Kami. According to legend, both Takemitsuguchi and Tsunetsunushi landed on the beach of Akashi, Tsunetsushi moved from there to Katori, and Takemitsuchi moved to the current main shrine {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=53-54}}.: The former main shrine of Numao Shrine was relocated from the inner shrine in 1619 (Genwa 5), ​​but the current main shrine was renovated in 1953 (Showa 28), and the worship hall has a gable. At the rear of the precincts, there are traces of the ``Numao Pond'' mentioned in the Fudoki {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=54}} (already depleted in the Edo period {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Gods)|1984}}). As mentioned later (section ``{{ill|lt=#Research|UNKNOWN|lt=Research}}''), there is a theory that this Numao Pond and Numao Shrine are the origin of the Kashima deity {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. The grounds of Numao Shrine are designated as a national historic site (included within the grounds of the main shrine) <ref name="historic site"/>. Furthermore, within the grounds of the main shrine there is a place of worship for Numao Shrine.

: "Ikisujinja". Kyoto Gaisetsusha. Kigami is said to be the god who led Takemikazuchi Okami from Izumo to Izumo when the country was being developed, and Amatorifunegami is the god who led Takemikazuchi Okami to Izumo when the country was transferred.{{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=56}}. ``Ikusu'' is a corruption of ``Okisu,'' which is said to derive from the fact that it was worshiped on an offshore island in the Katori Sea. </ref> (For details, see "{{ill|lt=Ikusu Shrine|Q11073095|qid=Q11073095|1=Ikisu Shrine}}").

=== Festival ===

=== Shikinen Festival ===
The ``Mifune Festival'' (Mifunesai) is held once every 12 years in {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=the year of the horse|1=UNKNOWN}} as the grand festival of Shikinen. {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=46}}. The Mifune Festival is said to have been turned into a festival during the era of {{ill|lt=Emperor Ojin|Q317997|qid=Q317997|1=Emperor Ōjin}}{{Sfn|Sadafumi Ueno|2002}}, and is said to be the biggest festival at the shrine {{Sfn|Shikinen Taisai (Kashima Shrine official website)}}. The festival is {{ill|lt=Sengoku period (Japan)|Q204023|qid=Q204023|lt=Abandoned during the Sengoku period|1=Sengoku period}}, it was revived in {{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}}3 ({{ill|lt=1870|Q7741|qid=Q7741|1=1870}}) {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}{{Sfn|Kashima Mifune Festival (National History)|1983}}.

The flow of the festival is as follows: {{Sfn|Shikinen Taisai (Kashima Shrine official website)}}{{Sfn|Sadafumi Ueno|2002}}.
* On the morning of September 1st, the annual festival was held in the presence of {{ill|lt=Emperor|Q11399920|qid=Q11399920|1=Chokushi}} sent by {{ill|lt=Emperor|Q208233|qid=Q208233|1=Emperor of Japan}}.* Early on the morning of the 2nd, the mikoshi departed from Kashima Shrine and arrived at Ofunazu on the shore of Lake {{ill|lt=Kasumigaura|Q1077984|qid=Q1077984|lt=Kitaura|1=Lake Kasumigaura}}. At Ofunazu, the mikoshi was placed on a gozabune decorated with dragon heads, and accompanied by many offering vessels, it was transported by water to {{ill|lt=Katori City|Q858357|qid=Q858357|1=Katori, Chiba}} Katozu. There, after receiving a welcoming ceremony at Katori Shrine, they return to the shrine via the same canal.
* On the afternoon of the 3rd, the shrine returned to the main shrine from the shrine.

; Hakuba Festival
: "Oumesai". {{ill|lt=January 7th|Q2228|qid=Q2228|1=January 7}}, Middle Festival.: In the past, at Jingu shrines, the festival was held off from New Year's Day until the 6th, as the enshrined deity was asleep, and on January 7th, when the enshrined deity woke up, the ``Otobiri Shinto Ritual'' was held to open the Fukaigoten (main shrine) as a memorial service.{{Sfn|Jingū Shi|2004|p=29-32}}. At that time, a white horse was quietly pulled around to ward off evil spirits, but gradually it began to be turned roughly so that the sound of the door key could not be heard. Nowadays, the door-opening ritual is no longer held, but instead, the ``Hakuba Festival'' is held in which a white horse runs from the east shrine gate to the tower gate.
; festival festival
: "Saitosai". {{ill|lt=March 9th|Q2401|qid=Q2401|1=March 9}}, Grand Festival.
: It is said to have started around the time of Emperor Tenmu, and is said to be a reproduction of the appearance of the warriors when they performed Kashima-tate.{{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Shikiuchisha)|1976}}. The festival is held in which two villages selected from among the 66 villages north and south of the Jingu (currently 24 Kitago and 26 Nango) perform services to the shrine. A colorful group led by Shibochi, who is about 5 years old, performs a festival parade in front of the shrine. The festival has been selected as a national {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Selected Intangible Folk Cultural Property|1=UNKNOWN}}.

Incidentally, the rituals at Kashima Jingu used to be garden rituals like those at Ise Jingu, but after the Meiji period, the rituals were changed to shrine rituals {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Shikinaisha)|1976}}.

=== Sacred Treasure ===
We will introduce two examples of sacred treasures that are extremely valued among Kashima Jingu Shrine. For other major sacred treasures, see the "{{ill|lt=#Cultural Properties|UNKNOWN|lt=Cultural Properties}}" section.

=== Dragon Spirit Sword ===
[[File:Isonokami-jingu, haiden-2.jpg|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|{{ill|lt=Ishigami Shrine|Q708859|qid=Q708859|1=Isonokami Jingū}} ({{jalin k|Nara Prefecture|Q131287}}{{ill|lt=Tenri City|Q502196|qid=Q502196|1=Tenri, Nara}})}}{{Small|It enshrines the Karareiken, which was given to Emperor Jinmu by the god Takemika Tsuchichi. On the Kashima Shrine side, this is the first generation {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=109}}. }}]]
``Futunomitama no Tsurugi'' (Futunomitama no Tsurugi) is a divine sword that has been passed down in the Jingu. Another name is "Kunimuke no Tsurugi" {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=108}}. It has been designated as a National Treasure, and its designated name is ``Chokuto, Kururushi Hyomon Tachigoshirae (Chokuto, Kurorushi Hyomon Tachigoshirae) with Sword Karaho'' <ref name="Naotou"/>. A <ref name="straight sword"/> that has been hidden in the inner sanctum of the main shrine as a sacred treasure since ancient times.It is a long straight sword, with a total length of 2.71 meters including the handle and scabbard, and a blade length of 2.24 meters. Although the year of production is uncertain, the blade is believed to be from the Nara period to the Heian period, and the koshirae is believed to be a work of the Heian period. It is one of the oldest traditional (not excavated) Japanese swords in existence, and is said to be the largest in terms of blade length. It has been discovered that in order to create a long blade, it uses an extremely rare method of joining the blades together at four points along the way, making it technically valuable. The exterior (handle and scabbard) is made using an old-fashioned technique of being decorated with black lacquer and hirimon (a technique of pasting thin plates of gold and silver to create patterns) and gilt-bronze openwork metal fittings, and is said to be descended from the ``Kingin-tōsō Kara-tai sword'' of Shosoin.{{ill|lt=Futomitama|Q11059754|qid=Q11059754|lt=Futunomitama|1=Futsu-no-mitama}} is also mentioned in "Kojiki" and "Nihonshoki" as "Karareiken" and "Futomitamaken", {{jalink|Emperor Jimmu|Q200 It is said to be a divine sword given to Iwarebiko ({{ill|lt=Emperor Jimmu|Q200188|qid=Q200188|1=Emperor Jimmu}}) by Takemikazuchi through {{ill|lt=Emperor Jinmu|Q200188|qid=Q200188|1=Emperor Jimmu}} in 188}}. This sword was enshrined in the Imperial Palace after Emperor Jinmu ascended the throne, and later during the reign of {{ill|lt=Emperor Sujin|Q333530|qid=Q333530|1=Emperor Sujin}} {{ill|lt=Ishigami Jingu|Q708859|qid=Q708859|1=Isonokami Jingū}} ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=UNKNOWN}}{{ill|lt=Tenri City|Q502196|qid=Q502196|1=Tenri, Nara}}) and is said to have been moved and enshrined there. </ref>. The Futsunomitama that has been handed down at Kashima Jingu Shrine is said to have been remade in later generations because, as mentioned above, the first Futsunomitama never returned to the Kashima deity. Regarding the making of swords, it has also been pointed out that there is a connection with the description of swords being made from iron sand in the Hitachi Province Fudoki <ref group="Hara" name="Fudōki"/><ref name="Naotō"/>.

=== Hitachi belt ===
'''Hitachi Obi'' (Hitachiobi) is a sacred treasure handed down at the shrine {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=72}}. It is said to be a belly belt that was dedicated by {{ill|lt=Empress Jingu|Q232803|qid=Q232803|1=Empress Jingū}} in gratitude for the protection of the Kashima deity during the {{ill|lt=Sankan Conquest|Q11249435|qid=Q11249435|1=Three Han Campaign}} {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=148}}. It has been kept in a box deep in the main shrine since ancient times, and even now it cannot be seen.{{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=72}}

Based on this tradition, the ``Hitachi Obi Shinto Ritual'' was once held on January 14th {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. During the festival, the ends of obi belts with the names of the man and woman written on them are offered before the shrine, and the priest ties them together to predict marriage.{{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Gods)|1984}} It can be found in the Takekawa volume of ``{{ill|lt=The Tale of Genji|Q8269|qid=Q8269|1=The Tale of Genji}}'' and ``{{ill|lt=Rokucho of Kokin Waka|Q11410888|qid=Q11410888|1=Kokin Waka Rokujō}}'' {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}, and it is already considered an old custom even in the Heian period {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Gods)|1984}}. Afterwards, this festival changed into a belief in safe childbirth, where pregnant women were given belly belts {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}.

=== Important cultural property (designated by the country) ===

References: ``National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties Buildings Official Report'', Cultural Properties and Buildings Preservation Technology Association, 1996; ``National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties Buildings Catalog'', Daiichi Hoki, 1990</ref>.* Setsusha Okumiya main hall (1 attached ridge plate) (building) - Designated on March 27, 1902 Kashima Jingu Setsusha Okumiya Main Hall (1 attached tag)] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.

* Plum and bamboo lacquered saddle (with four-handed lacquered wooden pair) (craft)*: Made in the Kamakura period, it is the oldest of {{ill|lt=Maki-e|Q2083390|qid=Q2083390|1=Maki-e}} Japanese saddles. In the shrine biography, there is an article in ``{{ill|lt=Azuma Kagami|Q1042324|qid=Q1042324|1=Azuma Kagami}}'' {{ill|lt=Kenkyu|Q1193933|qid=Q1193933|1=Kenkyū}} 2nd year ({{ill|lt=1191|Q19738|qid=Q19738|1=1191}})<ref group="hara">``Azuma Kagami'' December 26th, Kenkyu 2nd year (1191). </ref> describes it as a military saddle donated by Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800}}, but {{Sfn|Jingūshi|2004|p=73}} has a different style from normal military saddles, and it is assumed that it was used for festivals. Designated on June 27, 1955<ref>{{Nationally Designated Cultural Properties Database|201|5891|Ume-Chiku-Maki-e-kura}}<br />[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/kuni/kougei/4-9/4-9.html Ume-Chiku-Maki-e Kura] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.

=== Ibaraki Prefecture designated cultural property ===
[[File:Kashima-jingu tourou.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{Center|Stone lantern (Ibaraki Prefecture designated cultural property)}}]]
[[File:Kashima-jingu shasou.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{Center|Shrine complex in the shrine grounds<br />(Ibaraki Prefecture designated natural monument)}}]]
*Tangible cultural property
** 2 wooden guardian dogs (sculpture)
**: Created in 1619, early Edo period. Made of marquetry and lacquered leaf, the height of the A-type is 77.3 centimeters and the height of the Un-shaped is 80.3 centimeters. Designated on July 23, 1955 <ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/tyokoku/3-24/3-24.html Wooden guardian dog] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.
** 2 wooden guardian dogs (sculpture)
**: Made in the Kamakura period. Made of marquetry and lacquered leaf, each piece is 72 centimeters high. Designated on February 24, 1965 <ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/tyokoku/3-52/3-52.html Wooden guardian dog] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.
** 1 black lacquer mother-of-pearl makie table (craft)**: Late Kamakura period. Designated on July 23, 1955 <ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-23/4-23.html Black lacquer mother-of-pearl makie stand] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.
** Copper seal 1 piece (craft)
**: Made in the Heian period, the seal is "Shinda Takuin". There are two theories regarding the meaning of ``Shinda'': ``Kanda'' and ``God Seal.'' First seen in {{ill|lt=Ryokuō|Q1146182|qid=Q1146182|1=Ryakuō}}4 ({{ill|lt=1341|Q6062|qid=Q6062|1=1341}}), we can see examples of stamps being stamped on ancient documents. Designated on July 23, 1955 <ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-24/4-24.html Copper seal] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.
** Three ceramic guardian dogs (craft)
**: Appears to be a work of the Muromachi period. Designated on July 23, 1955 <ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-25/4-25.html Ceramic guardian dog] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.
** 1 stone lantern (craft)
**: Created in 1619, early Edo period. Height: 256 cm. Designated on July 23, 1955 <ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-26/4-26.html Stone Lantern] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.** 1 piece of iron (craft)
**: Sankotsugi made in the first half of the Heian period. Designated on July 23, 1955 <ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-27/4-27.html Tsui] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.
** Gunbai 1 piece (craft)
**: Created in the Muromachi period. Designated on July 23, 1955 <ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-28/4-28.html Gunbai] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.
** Tachi Mei Keiyasu 1 piece (craft)
**: This appears to have been made by Kageyasu, a Bizen swordsmith ({{ill|lt=Old Bizen school|Q11410932|qid=Q11410932|1=Ko-Bizen school}}) at the end of the Heian period. It was donated by Yorifusa Tokugawa, the first lord of Mito. Height is 77.5cm. Designated on March 24, 1963 <ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-34/4-34.html Tachi (signed Keiyasu)] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.
** 1 mirror with flowers and twin birds (craft)
**: Created in the Muromachi period. It was stolen in 1970 (undiscovered). Designated on February 24, 1965 <ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-63/4-63.html Flowers and Twin Birds Round Mirror] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.
** 11-faced Kannon's true form (craft)**: Created in the early Kamakura period. It was stolen in 1970 (undiscovered). Designated on February 24, 1965 <ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/kougei/4-64/4-64.html Eleven-faced Kannon Goji] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.
** Kashima Jingu Documents Volume 18 (Ancient Documents)
**: A total of 250 ancient documents, from Minamoto no Yoritomo's manuscript dated 2nd year ({{ill|lt=Genryaku|Q1194250|qid=Q1194250|1=Genryaku}} ({{ill|lt=1185|Q19729|qid=Q19729|1=1185}}) to the Jingikan datsusho ({{ill|lt=1871|Q7746|qid=Q7746|1=1871}}). It is made into 18 scrolls. Designated November 10, 2010 <ref>[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/komon/6-6/6-6.html Kashima Jingu Documents] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.
* Natural monument
** Kashima Jingu Trees - Designated August 23, 1960 <ref name="trees">[http://www.edu.pref.ibaraki.jp/board/bunkazai/ken/tennen/14-28/14-28.html Kashima Shrine Trees] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>.

=== Related matters ===

=== Kashima Gunga ===
[[File:Kashimaguuke-ato -3.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Kannomukai Ruins (Kashima City Miyanaka)}}]]
{{ill|lt=Kashima County (Ibaraki Prefecture)|Q6374307|qid=Q6374307|lt=Kashima County|1=Kashima District, Ibaraki}} (Koshima County) is located in the "Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki" <ref group="Hara" name="Fudoki">"Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki" Kashima District (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). According to </ref>, the internal affairs of {{ill|lt=Shimokai Kunizo|Q11361123|qid=Q11361123|lt=Kamigami Kunizo|1=Shimotsu Unakami no Kuni Miyatsuko}} of {{ill|lt=Shimosa Province|Q1053695|qid=Q1053695|1=Shimōsa Province}} and {{ill|lt=Nakakunizo|Q1 1378492|qid=Q1 1378492|lt=Nagakunizo}} It is said that the county was established from the beginning as {{ill|lt=Kamigun|Q11590937|qid=Q11590937|1=Kamigun}} from the beginning {{Sfn|Kashima County (Kadokawa)|1983}}. No remains of the old Gunga have been found, {{Sfn|Kashima-gun (Kadokawa)|1983}}, and since it is the Gunga of Kami-gun, it is assumed that it is near a shrine {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Gods)|1984}}.The Shingunga ruins dating from the 8th century onwards are the ``Kanomukai Ruins'' in Miyanaka, Kashima City, located approximately 1.5 km south of the shrine. 9|N|140|38|01.67|E|region:JP-08_type:landmark|name=Discovered at Kashima County Family Ruins (Kannomukai Ruins)}}). The remains consist of the inner fort of the county office, a facility equivalent to a kitchen, Shosoin, etc. dating from the early 8th century to the early 10th century. This location also matches the description in the "Hitachi Province Fudoki" <ref group="Hara" name="Fudoki"/> that the county residence is located ``south of that shrine.'' The ruins are designated as a national historic site as an adjunct to the precincts of Kashima Shrine. Visiting Hitachi Province Fudoki - 1300th Anniversary of Hitachi Province Fudoki (Ibaraki Prefecture Living Environment Department Lifestyle Culture Division's ``I love Ibaraki Lifestyle Culture Information Net'')</ref><ref name="Historical Site"/>.

Since Kashima Shrine was a base for the development of eastern Japan, its descendant deities, or {{ill|lt=Mikogami|Q352176|qid=Q352176|1=Mikogami}}, were formed in various places{{Sfn|Kashima Migo Shrine (National History)|1983}}. ``Hitachi Province Fudoki'' <ref group="Hara" name="Namegata District">``Hitachi Province Fudoki'' Namegata District. By the time of </ref>, the existence of a branch shrine was already recorded in {{ill|lt=Namegata County (Ibaraki Prefecture)|Q11626140|qid=Q11626140|lt=Namegata County|1=Namegata District, Ibaraki}} {{Sfn|Kashima Migo Shrine (National History)|1983}}.

An article about the 8th year of Jogan ({{ill|lt=866|Q23872|qid=Q23872|1=866}}) in the ``Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku'' ({{ill|lt=866|Q23872|qid=Q23872|1=866}}).<ref name="Jōgan 8" group="hara"> Article on the 20th day of the New Year in the 8th year of Jogan (866) in the ``Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku'' (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). In </ref>, it is stated that there are 38 shrines dedicated to Naesei-kami in Mutsu Province, according to the words of the chief priest {{Sfn|Kashima Migo Shrine (National History)|1983}}. The details are as follows, but the specific company names are not listed {{Sfn|Oise Shrine (Gods)|1984}}.: {{ill|lt=Kikuta-gun|Q11619613|qid=Q11619613|1=Kikuta district}} 1, {{ill|lt=Iwaki-gun|Q11587876|qid=Q11587876|1=Iwaki district}} 11, {{ill|lt=Obeha-gun|Q11542238|qid=Q11542238|1=Shineha district}} 2,
: {{ill|lt=Namegata County (Fukushima Prefecture)|Q11626139|qid=Q11626139|lt=Namegata County|1=Namekata district}} 1, {{ill|lt=Uta County|Q11449246|qid=Q11449246|1=Uda district}} 7, {{ill|lt=Igu County|Q1155531|qid=Q1155531|1=Igu District, Miyagi}} 1,
: {{ill|lt=Watari-gun|Q1131765|qid=Q1131765|lt=Eri-gun|1=Watari District, Miyagi}} 2, {{ill|lt=Miyagi-gun|Q1131751|qid=Q1131751|1=Miyagi District}} 3, {{ill|lt=Kurokawa-gun|Q1131782|qid=Q1131782|lt=Kurokawa-gun|1=Kurokawa District, Miyagi}} 1,
: Shikama-gun 3, {{ill|lt=Shida-gun|Q7496121|qid=Q7496121|lt=Shida-gun|1=Shida District, Miyagi}} 1, {{ill|lt=Oda-gun (Mutsu Province)|Q11463188|qid=Q11463188|lt=Oda-gun|1=Oda District}} 4,
: {{ill|lt=Oshika-gun|Q1131921|qid=Q1131921|1=Oshika District, Miyagi}} 1
The same article also states that the curse of the Kashima deity in Mutsu Province was so severe that in the first year of {{ill|lt=Kasho|Q1373157|qid=Q1373157|1=Kashō}} ({{ill|lt=848|Q30380|qid=Q30380|1=848}}) the chief priests went to worship the shrine, but they were not allowed to enter Mutsu Province.{{Sfn|Oise Shrine (Gods)|1984}}. Regarding this, there is a theory that the branch shrine resisted because the clan performing the rituals at the shrine had changed {{Sfn|Oise Shrine (Gods)|1984}}.In addition, "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" {{ill|lt=Engishiki Shinmyocho|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932|lt=Shinmyocho|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō}}<ref group="Hara" name="Mutsu">'Engishiki' Shinmyocho Mutsu Kunijo. In </ref>, the following eight shrines are listed as shrines with the name ``Kashima'' in the Articles of Mutsu Province (see ``{{ill|lt=List of Shikinai Shrines in Mutsu Province|Q11658590|qid=Q11658590|1=List of Shikinaisha in Mutsu Province}}'').

|}{{-}}From the above description, it can be seen that Kashima no Kami moved north along the coast to Oshika District (near present-day Miyagi Prefecture {{ill|lt=Ishinomaki City|Q270814|qid=Q270814|1=Ishinomaki}}) {{Sfn|Kashima Migo Shrine (National History)|1983}}. From the name of the shrine, it is also inferred that "{{ill|lt=Amagoyane-no-Mikoto|UNKNOWN|lt=Tensokubetsu-no-Mikoto}}" exists as a child deity of the Kashima god. </ref>. In the "Engishiki" divine name book <ref group="Hara" name="Mutsu"/>, you can also see the two Naesen-jin shrines of Katori Shrine, but see <ref> "{{ill|lt=Katori Shrine #Katori Naesen-jin|Q372380|qid=Q372380|1=Katori Jingū}}". </ref>, the existence of these Kashima and Katori Naegojin is interpreted to be because the forces of the Yamato court looked up to the divine power of both Kashima and Katori when they advanced north along the coast {{Sfn|Kashima Migo Shrine (National History)|1983}}. The specific circumstances are that Omisayama no Mikoto, a distant ancestor of the {{ill|lt=Nakatomi clan|Q1198447|qid=Q1198447|1=Nakatomi clan}}, participated in {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Waken no Mikoto|1=UNKNOWN}}'s eastern expedition activities, and the Kashima deity, which is often seen in the Mutsu region, The distribution of mikogami appears to be due to the fact that the ancestors of the Nakatomi clan and people related to the tribe accompanied and engaged in eastern expedition activities. Descendants of ancient Urabe who were responsible for fortune-telling,” Aogaki Publishing, 2014, pp. 36-37. </ref>.A related event is '''{{ill|lt=Shigama Shrine|Q133753|qid=Q133753|1=Shiogama shrine}}''' in Ichinomiya, Mutsu Province (Miyagi Prefecture {{ill|lt=Shiogama City|Q496448|qid=Q496448|1=Shiogama}}, {{Coord|38|19|08.12|N|141|00|45.4 7|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|name=Mutsu Province Ichinomiya: Shiogama Shrine (both Takemikazuchi and Tsunetsunushi deities are enshrined)}}) also enshrines Takemikazuchi and Tsunetsunushi deities {{Sfn|Kashima Mikoto Shrine (National History) | 1983}}. Furthermore, there is a difference in the distribution of Kashima and Katori, and the two Katori Naesenjin shrines are enshrined in positions that jump over Kashima {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Gods)|1984}}. Based on this, there is a theory that in the early stages, Kashima was oriented towards the Sotome (Ezo) and Katori towards the Inland Sea ({{ill|lt=Katorikai|Q11667182|qid=Q11667182|1=Katori Sea}}), but later the divine authority of the two gods reversed {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Gods)|1984}}.

In addition, in later generations, Kashima-jin was worshiped as a god of war and was worshiped in various places, and many branch shrines were formed throughout the country, mainly in the former Hitachi Province region.

=== Kashima Seven Wonders ===
Kashima Jingu Shrine has what is called the ``Seven Wonders'', and the following seven items are listed {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Heibonsha)|1982}}.
* {{ill|lt=#Keystone|UNKNOWN|lt=Keystone}}
* {{ill|lt=#Mitarai Pond|UNKNOWN|lt=Water depth of Mitarai Pond}}
* Suenashi River - It is said that the water that gushes out in Takamagahara outside the precincts cannot be traced {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=192-193}}.
* Wisteria flowers on Mt. Mikasa in the temple grounds - Years in which a lot of wisteria blooms are said to be a good harvest, and years in which there are few blooms are said to be a bad harvest. {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=192-193}}.
* Kashima Sea Sea Sound - It is said that when the sound of waves can be heard to the north (especially near Okumiya), it will be sunny, and when it can be heard to the south, it will rain.{{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=192-193}}
* Neagari no Matsu - It is said that no matter how many times the pine trees of Jingu are cut down, they will sprout and never wither. {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=192-193}}
* Pine chopsticks - Chopsticks made from Jingu pine are said to produce no fat. {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=192-193}}.

=== Historical evidence ===

=== Ruins/tumuli ===
[[File:Meotozuka-kofun (Kashima).JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|[[Meotozuka Kofun (Kashima City)|Meotozuka Kofun]] (Kashima City Miyanaka)}}{{Small|The largest tumulus in the Miyanakano kofun group, built around the middle to late 6th century. }}]]
Many {{ill|lt=Jomon period|Q52824|qid=Q52824|1=Jōmon period}} ruins have been found around Kashima, but there are only a few {{ill|lt=Yayoi period|Q207858|qid=Q207858|1=Yayoi period}} ruins {{Sfn|Tomomi|2000|p=85}}. Even in the {{ill|lt=Kofun period|Q459939|qid=Q459939|1=Kofun period}}, no old burial mounds have been found, and among the ritual artifacts found within the shrine grounds, the pottery excavated is said to be from the 6th century or later {{Sfn|Seiji Okada|2011}}.Regarding the burial mounds related to the shrine, there are more than 100 ancient tombs, including 17 {{ill|lt=keyhole-shaped tombs|Q11268718|qid=Q11268718|1=Zenpō-kōen-fun}}, located 2 kilometers to the northeast. The ``Miyanakano Kofun Group,'' which consists of </ref>, is known. The group of tombs is said to have been constructed between the 6th and 7th centuries, and among them is {{ill|lt=Meotozuka tumulus. (Kashima City)|Q24903013|qid=Q24903013|lt=Meotozuka Kofun|1=Meotozuka Kofun}} (Kashima City designated historic site, {{Coord|35|58|56.39|N|140|36|41.41|E|region: JP-08_type:landmark|name=Meotozuka Kofun (Miyanakano Kofun Group)}}) is a keyhole-shaped tumulus with a length of approximately 108 meters, which is the largest of the kofun group<ref name="Meotozuka"/>. Other major burial mounds include the Otsuka Tumulus (Tokuzuka), which is {{ill|lt=scallop-shaped tumulus|Q11480883|qid=Q11480883|lt=scallop-style keyhole-shaped tumulus|1=Scallop-shaped kofun}}. This group of burial mounds is considered to be a group of chief tombs in the Kashima region, <ref name="Meotozuka"/>, and it has also been pointed out that there is a relationship with Kashima Jingu Shrine. </ref>. In addition, there is an 80-meter-long ancient tomb called Onizuka in Takamagahara to the east of the shrine. 0598}}It has been pointed out that the {{ill|lt=Ouse Tumulus Group|Q17221219|qid=Q17221219|1=Ōu-kofungun}} located in Oobu is also related to Kashima Jingu {{Sfn|Ooya Shrine (Gods)|1984}}.In addition, large-scale village ruins have been discovered in the Kuridai ruins in Kashima City, and the excavation of pottery with ink writing by ``Kashima Gocho'' and ``Nakatomi Takunari'' indicates that this area is recognized as the center of Kashima-go, Kashima-gun, and the residence of the Nakatomi clan. It has also been pointed out that the increase in the number of pit buildings in the mid-7th century corresponded to the increase of 50 houses in Kobe during the reign of Emperor Kotoku (645-654). “Archaeology of Gods and the Dead: Ancient Festivals and Beliefs” (History and Culture Library 417), Yoshikawa Kobunkan, 2016, pp. 53-56. </ref>.

=== About the original place ===
[[File:Taya, Kashima, Ibaraki.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Scenery of Taya, Kashima City}}{{Small|Around the ruins of Numao Pond. }}]]
Kashima Jingu is located in a strategic location and is said to have come under the control of the Yamato government at a very early stage because it was the base of the Yamato government's control over eastern Japan.{{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (National History)|1983}} According to "Hitachikuni Fudoki" <ref group="Hara" name="Fudoki"/>, Kashima Jingu Shrine is described as ``Koshima's Heavenly Deity,'' which is the collective name for the following three shrines.{{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Gods)|1984}}
* '''Ame-no-Okami-no-Yashiro'' (Ame-no-Okami-no-Yashiro) - Current Kashima Jingu Shrine (main shrine).
* '''Sakato no Yashiro'' (Sakato no Yashiro) - The current Sakato Shrine, a shrine outside the precincts.
* '''Numao Shrine'' (Numao no Yashiro) - The current external shrine Numao Shrine.
It is said that in ancient times it was a shrine consisting of three shrines, and in the "Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki" <ref group="Hara" name="Fudoki"/> there is also a description (the origin story of the Mifune Festival) that three boats were dedicated during the reign of Emperor Keiko {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Gods)|1984}}.Of these three shrines, a theory has been proposed for a long time that the origin of the shrine is somewhere other than ``Ama no Okami Shrine''. According to the theory that ``Numao Shrine'' is the original source, it is presumed that the nearby ``Numao Pond'' was once worshiped as a god. The basis for this is that in "Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki" <ref group="Hara" name="Fudoki"/>, Numao Pond is described as ``a swamp filled with water that flowed from the sky,'' and it is thought that it was a god that fell from the sky. On the other hand, the basis for the theory that it is ``Sakado Shrine'' is based on the writing order of ``Sakado-Numao'' in the ``Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki'' and the assumption that Kogunga, which should be near the shrine, is ``Yamanoue'' where Sakado Shrine is enshrined {{Sfn|Kashima Shrine (Gods)|1984}}. Regarding the meaning of the company name ``Sakado'', it has been pointed out that ``Saka'' means ``boundary'' and that it means ``the boundary/entrance to Ezochi'' {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Gods)|1984}}.

=== About the enshrined deity and the enshrined clan ===
[[File:Ōu-jinja shaden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|{{ill|lt=Osei Shrine|Q17221225|qid=Q17221225|1=Ōu Shrine}} ({{ill|lt=Itako City|Q840598|qid=Q840598|1=Itako, Ibaraki}}Osei)}}{{Small|Tell them that it is the former shrine of Kashima. }}]]
'''{{ill|lt=Nakatomi clan|Q1198447|qid=Q1198447|1=Nakatomi clan}}''' is known as the clan that performs rituals at Kashima Shrine. The Nakatomi clan had already been active since the time it appeared in history books, and the {{ill|lt=Fujiwara clan|Q641628|qid=Q641628|1=Fujiwara clan}}, which descended from the Nakatomi clan, also worshiped the shrine as its guardian deity. Existing genealogies show that the Nakatomi clan produced the chief priests of Kashima Jingu Shrine, and there is also an article in ``{{ill|lt=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki|Q11481687|qid=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}'' about the family worshiping the Kashima deity. On the other hand, there is a theory that the Nakatomi clan came to be in charge of the shrine because the Nakatomi clan, which was in charge of central rituals, reorganized the shrine in response to the Imperial Court's request to strengthen the management of the eastern region, and another theory that it was due to the decline of the primitive ritual clan {{Sfn|Seiji Okada|2011}}. In that case, there are two theories regarding the time when they took control: {{Sfn|Seiji Okada|2011}}, and another theory says it was at the time when Nakatomi was given the surname of Kashima (746). Among those who believe that the Nakatomi clan was not the original clan in charge, there is the following theory regarding the clans that performed rituals before the Nakatomi clan took control.

; {{ill|lt=Taji|Q11430816|qid=Q11430816|1=Ō clan}} theory: The theory is that the clans before the Nakatomi clan were divided into multiple clans, and the basis for this is that '''{{ill|lt=Oio Shrine|Q17221225|qid=Q17221225|1=Ōu Shrine}}''' ({{ill|lt=Itako City|Q840598|qid=Q840598|1=Itako, Ibaraki}}Osei, {{Coord|35|59|30.54|N|140|33|06.43|E|region:JP-08_type:landmark|name=Osei Shrine (also known as Kashima Hongu Shrine)}}) exists {{Sfn|Oise Shrine (Gods)|1984}}. It is said that the company's name ``Oou'' came from the residence of the Taji clan, and there is also a legend that it was solicited from {{ill|lt=Tazaya Shirituhiko Shrine|Q11430652|qid=Q11430652|lt=Tajinja|1=Oonimasumishiritsuhiko Shrine}} (home of the Taji clan) in Nara. Furthermore, it is said that a monk from Kashima Shrine was brought to the annual festival of Oio Shrine, but the monk only takes part in six of the shrine's festivals a year (Section {{ill|lt=#Shinto|UNKNOWN|lt=Shinto}}). The fact that Oio Shrine outside the precincts occupied one of them is an extraordinary treatment. </ref>. An ancient document about Oise Shrine states that Kashima Jingu changed its character with the establishment of Kasuga Taisha Shrine, and that Oise Shrine was involved in this {{Sfn|Oise Shrine (Gods)|1984}}. A group of burial mounds ({{ill|lt=Ouse Kofun Group|Q17221219|qid=Q17221219|1=Ōu-kofungun}}) from the middle of the Kofun period (5th century) remain around this Ooya Shrine, and are said to be the tombs of the clans performing shrine rituals. Ouse Kofun Group] (Ibaraki Prefectural Board of Education). </ref>, it has also been pointed out that each keyhole-shaped tumulus faces either Oo-jinja Shrine or Kashima-jingu Shrine {{Sfn|Oo-jinja Shrine (Gods)|1984}}.: Regarding the Ta clan, there are the {{ill|lt=Nakakunizo|Q11378492|qid=Q11378492|1=Naka no Kuni no Miyatsuko}} who ruled the Naka region before the division of Kashima County, and the Kunizo of Iwaki District, Mutsu Province (Dooku Ishijokuni It is also pointed out that all of them were of the {{ill|lt=Kamiyaimimi no Mikoto|Q11588756|qid=Q11588756|1=Kamuyaimimi}} lineage of many ancestors {{Sfn|Oise Shrine (Gods)|1984}}.
:On the other hand, the {{ill|lt=tutelary deity|Q767655|qid=Q767655|1=Ujigami}} has been the {{ill|lt=ancestral deity|Q85882782|qid=Q85882782|1=Oyagami}} of a blood-related group since ancient times, and as a general rule, the deity is enshrined by the clan of the descendants. </ref><ref>Yasutoshi Koike, “The Book on the Correct Family Affairs that Japanese People Should Know,” President Publishing, 2015, 89 pages. </ref>, and in genealogy historical materials, Takemi Raijin is positioned as the ancestral deity of the Nakatomi clan. </ref>. According to this, it is clear that the Ta clan is not a descendant of Takemikaraijin, and there is no example of the Ta clan enshrining Takemikazujin in areas where other clans lived (Owari Province, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shino Province|1=UNKNOWN}}, etc.). In addition, it is pointed out from the tradition of {{ill|lt=Akiru Shrine|Q11657213|qid=Q11657213|1=Akiru Shrine}} that the ancestors of the Tamatsukuri and Nakatomi clans came to Musashi during the Sujin Dynasty, and the Tamatsukuri clan expanded to the Mutsu region. </ref>, as it is possible that there was a large distribution of Urabe in Mutsu based on the recent excavation of wooden tablets, it seems that this ritual was performed by people related to the Nakatomi clan (Urabe clan).<ref name="#1"/>; {{ill|lt=Mr. Mononobe|Q1755836|qid=Q1755836|1=Mononobe clan}} theory
: According to the theory that the Mononobe clan is a primitive ritual clan, due to the relationship between {{ill|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi|Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|1=Takemikazuchi}}, Kareiken, and Ishigami Shrine, the theory that Takemikazuchi is the god worshiped by the Mononobe clan{{Sfn|Seiji Okada|2011}}. Among them, it is said that the Mononobe clan went on expeditions to various places in worship of Futsunomitama between the 5th and 6th centuries, and it is explained that the {{ill|lt=Musashi Kokuzo Rebellion|Q11546341|qid=Q11546341|1=Musashi Kokuzo Rebellion}} that occurred in the 6th century coincides with the request for the establishment of a guardian deity in the eastern region {{Sfn|Seiji Okada|2011}}.

The enshrined deity of Kashima Shrine has been Takemikazuchi since ancient times, but there is no direct mention of Takemikazuchi as the enshrined deity in the Kojiki, Nihon Shoki, or Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki. It goes all the way to the ``Kogo Shui'' (compiled in 807) or the ``Kasuga Festival Norito'' (compiled between 768 and 927) included in the Engishiki (section ``{{ill|lt=#Enshrined God|UNKNOWN|lt=Enshrined God}}'').Those who do not view Kashima-no-kami as Takemikazuchi believe that the reason for the establishment of the enshrined deity is that the Nakatomi clan substituted Takemikazuchi for the god of primitive rituals as the Yamato government proceeded with the management of eastern Japan. On the other hand, as mentioned above, there is a view that Takemikazuchi is a god worshiped by the Mononobe clan {{Sfn|Seiji Okada|2011}}, and there are also indications that it is the name of a god and the tradition of ``Mika = Jar'' that remains in Kashima {{Sfn|Kashima Jingu (Gods)|1984}}. There is a theory that Takemikazuchi took root in Hitachi not far back in the 8th century. </ref>. On the other hand, the names of the distant ancestors of the Nakatomi clan, such as {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hinokagu Tsuchijin|1=UNKNOWN}} and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hamanoyasubiurijin|1=UNKNOWN}}, are associated with the clay of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Tenkoguyama|1=UNKNOWN}}, and are the ancestors of pots made from clay and Takemikazuchi. There is also a theory that the tradition of the pot is supporting evidence that it is the guardian deity of the Nakatomi clan, as it is related to {{ill|lt=Oghasahijin|Q11574224|qid=Q11574224|1=Mika-haya-hi}}. </ref>.In addition, from the other name of the deity enshrined at Katori Shrine, ``Ihahinushi (Iwainushi, Ihabishu/Saiku)'', there is another name for both Kashima and Katori Shrines: ``Kashima = the god of the imperial court'', and ``Katori = the god of the imperial court''. It has also been pointed out that it is a ritual similar to the inner and outer shrines of {{ill|lt=Ise Grand Shrine|Q687168|qid=Q687168|1=Ise Grand Shrine}}, called ``Local Gods (servant gods)''.

'''Access'''
* Railway
** {{ill|lt=East Japan Railway|Q499071|qid=Q499071|1=East Japan Railway Company}} (JR East) {{ill|lt=Kashima Line|Q5370725|qid=Q5370725|1=Kashima Line}} "{{ill|lt=Kashima Jingu Station|Q5359650|qid=Q5359650|1=Kashimajingū Station}}" (10 minutes walk) - {{ill|lt=Kashima Rinkai Railway|Q5370740|qid=Q5370740|1=Kashima Rinkai Railway}}{{ill|lt=Kashima Rinkai Railway Oarai Kashima Line|Q6374313|qid=Q6374313|lt=Oarai Kashima Line|1=Ōarai Kashima Line}} is also available.
*Highway bus
**From the central Tokyo area ({{ill|lt=Tokyo Station|Q283196|qid=Q283196|1=Tokyo Station}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Haneda Airport|1=UNKNOWN}}, {{ill|lt=Tokyo Teleport Station|Q906738|qid=Q906738|1=Tokyo Teleport Station}}), get off at the express bus "{{ill|lt=Kashima Bus Terminal|Q11677087|qid=Q11677087|lt=Kashima Jingu|1=Kashima Bus Terminal}}" bus stop (7 minutes walk). (Be careful not to confuse it with the next bus stop, "Kashima-Jingu Station.")
* car
** From the Tokyo/Chiba area, take {{ill|lt=Higashi-Kanto Expressway|Q864875|qid=Q864875|1=Higashi-Kantō Expressway}} {{ill|lt=Itako Interchange|Q11565707|qid=Q11565707|lt=Itako IC|1=Itako interchange}} and take {{ill|lt=National Route 51|Q855484|qid=Q855484|1=Japan National Route 51}} towards Kashima for about 20 minutes.** From the Choshi/Kamisu area, take {{ill|lt=National Route 124|Q11421405|qid=Q11421405|1=Japan National Route 124}}, and from the Mito area, take National Route 51.
** Parking: In addition to Kashima-Jingu Parking Lots 1 and 2 (charges apply), municipal parking lots (charges apply) are scattered around Kashima-Jingu Station.
